````math
- \[1\] S. Gopi, P. Gulhane, J. Kulkarni, J. H. Shen, M. Shokouhi, and
  S. Yekhanin. Differentially private set union. *ICML*, 2020. Journal
  version in *Journal of Privacy and Confidentiality*.

## Appendix B On the Limits of Contractive Policies for Differentially Private Set Union

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.1 Introduction

Differentially private set union (DPSU) is a fundamental primitive in
private data analysis. Given a database of $`n`$ users, where each user
$`i`$ holds a subset $`W_{i}`$ of items from a universe $`U`$, the goal
is to output a large subset $`S\subseteq\bigcup_{i}W_{i}`$ while
satisfying $`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-differential privacy. This problem
arises in vocabulary extraction, $`n`$-gram discovery, search query
release, and many natural language processing applications \[[Korolova
et al.(2009)](#bibb.bibx7), [Wilson et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx8), [Gopi
et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\].

Gopi et al. \[[Gopi et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\] introduced the
*contractive policy* framework. In particular, an
$`\ell_{2}`$-contractive update policy yields a histogram with
$`\ell_{2}`$-sensitivity at most $`1`$, which can then be released
privately via the Gaussian mechanism. They proposed two policies: the
$`\ell_{2}`$-descent (Algorithm 7) and the $`\ell_{1}`$-descent
(Algorithm 8). The $`\ell_{1}`$-descent achieves the best empirical
performance and is claimed to be $`\ell_{2}`$-contractive in
Proposition 5.1.

##### Our contributions.

1.  1.
    Counterexample to Proposition 5.1. We show that the
    $`\ell_{1}`$-descent policy is *not* $`\ell_{2}`$-contractive: there
    exist neighboring databases where the histogram’s
    $`\ell_{2}`$-sensitivity exceeds $`1`$
    (Section [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Counterexample to Proposition 5.1 ‣ Appendix B On the Limits of Contractive Policies for Differentially Private Set Union ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")).
    We identify the specific error in the proof: the Jacobian of the
    $`\ell_{1}`$-descent map is block *lower triangular* (not block
    diagonal), and its spectral norm exceeds $`1`$ whenever any item
    reaches the cutoff $`\Gamma`$.
2.  2.
    Barrier for Policy Gaussian. We isolate the main bottleneck in the
    Policy Gaussian proof
    (Section [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 A Barrier within the Policy Gaussian Framework ‣ Appendix B On the Limits of Contractive Policies for Differentially Private Set Union ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")):
    for $`t`$ equally situated fresh spillover items, symmetry and an
    $`\ell_{2}`$-budget of $`1`$ force per-item weight at most
    $`1/\sqrt{t}`$. On the corresponding equal-spillover/full-budget
    instances, the $`\ell_{2}`$-descent attains this bound. Thus any
    substantial improvement of that proof step within the same
    support-conditioning template must either intentionally give fresh
    items less weight or rely on a different mechanism or privacy proof.
3.  3.
    Numerical illustration. We quantify the resulting spillover
    surcharge on a Zipf benchmark. The surcharge is modest for smaller
    values of $`\varepsilon`$, but it grows as the Gaussian noise
    shrinks.

These results suggest that, among Gopi et al.’s two named contractive
policies, the $`\ell_{2}`$-descent is the one currently supported by a
correct $`\ell_{2}`$-privacy proof and matches the spillover barrier
analyzed in
Section [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 A Barrier within the Policy Gaussian Framework ‣ Appendix B On the Limits of Contractive Policies for Differentially Private Set Union ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
on the corresponding equal-spillover/full-budget instances, whereas the
empirically stronger $`\ell_{1}`$-descent lacks a valid
$`\ell_{2}`$-privacy guarantee.

### B.2 Preliminaries

###### Definition B.1 (Differential Privacy \[[Dwork et al.(2006)](#bibb.bibx3), [Dwork and Roth(2014)](#bibb.bibx4)\]).

A randomized algorithm $`\mathcal{A}`$ is
$`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-differentially private if for all neighboring
databases $`D\sim D^{\prime}`$ (differing in one user) and all
measurable sets $`\mathcal{S}`$:
$`\Pr[\mathcal{A}(D)\in\mathcal{S}]\leq e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[\mathcal{A}(D^{\prime})\in\mathcal{S}]+\delta.`$

###### Definition B.2 (DPSU Problem).

Given $`n`$ users with subsets $`W_{i}\subseteq U`$ and a contribution
bound $`\Delta_{0}=\max_{i}|W_{i}|`$, design an
$`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-DP algorithm outputting
$`S\subseteq\bigcup_{i}W_{i}`$ with $`|S|`$ as large as possible.

###### Proposition B.3 (Gaussian Mechanism \[[Balle and Wang(2018)](#bibb.bibx1)\]).

If $`f`$ has $`\ell_{2}`$-sensitivity $`\Delta_{2}`$, the mechanism
$`M(D)=f(D)+Z`$, $`Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I)`$, is
$`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-DP if and only if
$`\Phi\bigl(\frac{\Delta_{2}}{2\sigma}-\frac{\varepsilon\sigma}{\Delta_{2}}\bigr)-e^{\varepsilon}\Phi\bigl(-\frac{\Delta_{2}}{2\sigma}-\frac{\varepsilon\sigma}{\Delta_{2}}\bigr)\leq\delta.`$

We write $`\sigma^{*}(\varepsilon,\delta,\Delta_{2})`$ for the minimum
$`\sigma`$ satisfying the Balle–Wang inequality above.

##### The contractive policy framework \[[Gopi et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\].

Algorithm 2 of the original paper builds a weighted histogram $`H`$ by
iterating over users in a random hash order. Each user $`i`$ updates the
histogram using an *update policy* $`\phi`$ with $`\ell_{2}`$-budget 1
(i.e., $`\left\lVert\phi(H,W_{i})-H\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1`$). If
$`\phi`$ is $`\ell_{2}`$-*contractive*—meaning there exists an invariant
set
$`\mathcal{I}\subset\{(H_{1},H_{2}):\left\lVert H_{1}-H_{2}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1\}`$
satisfying the two properties in Definition 1.3 of \[[Gopi
et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\]—then the histogram has
$`\ell_{2}`$-sensitivity $`\leq 1`$ (Theorem 1.1). Adding Gaussian noise
$`\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})`$ and thresholding at $`\rho`$ yields
Algorithm 1, the meta-algorithm for DPSU.

##### Two policies.

- •
  $`\ell_{2}`$-descent (Algorithm 7): move $`H|_{W}`$ toward
  $`(\Gamma,\ldots,\Gamma)`$ by $`\ell_{2}`$-distance $`\leq 1`$. Proved
  $`\ell_{2}`$-contractive in Lemma 5.2 of \[[Gopi
  et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\] via a geometric argument (Lemma 5.1).
- •
  $`\ell_{1}`$-descent (Algorithm 8): maximize $`\sum_{u}y_{u}`$ subject
  to $`y_{u}\leq\Gamma`$ and
  $`\left\lVert y-H|_{W}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1`$. *Claimed*
  $`\ell_{2}`$-contractive in Proposition 5.1 of \[[Gopi
  et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\] via a Jacobian argument.

##### Privacy of the Policy Gaussian algorithm (Theorem 5.1 of \[[Gopi et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\]).

With an $`\ell_{2}`$-contractive symmetric policy,
sensitivity $`\leq 1`$, noise parameter

|     |                                                          |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \sigma=\sigma^{*}(\varepsilon,\delta_{\mathrm{mech}},1),
       ```                                                       |     | (1) |

and threshold

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho=\max_{1\leq t\leq\Delta_{0}}\Bigl(\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}+\sigma\,\Phi^{-1}\bigl((1-\delta_{\mathrm{spill}})^{1/t}\bigr)\Bigr),
``` |  | (2) |

where $`\delta_{\mathrm{mech}}+\delta_{\mathrm{spill}}=\delta`$, the
algorithm is $`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-DP. The paper sets
$`\delta_{\mathrm{mech}}=\delta_{\mathrm{spill}}=\delta/2`$.

### B.3 Counterexample to Proposition 5.1

###### Theorem B.4 (Proposition 5.1 of \[[Gopi et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\] is false).

The $`\ell_{1}`$-descent policy (Algorithm 8 of \[[Gopi
et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\]) is not $`\ell_{2}`$-contractive. In
particular, there exist neighboring databases $`D_{1},D_{2}`$ and a
cutoff $`\Gamma`$ such that the histograms $`H_{1},H_{2}`$ produced by
Algorithm 2 with the $`\ell_{1}`$-descent policy satisfy
$`\left\lVert H_{1}-H_{2}\right\rVert_{2}>1`$.

###### Proof.

We exhibit a concrete instance. Let $`U=\{a,b,c\}`$, $`\Gamma=5`$,
$`\Delta_{0}=3`$, and define:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle D_{1}`$ | $`\displaystyle=[\{a,b,c\},\ \{a,b\},\ \{a,b\},\ \{b,c\},\ \{b,c\},\ \{b,c\},\ \{b,c\},\ \{b,c\}],`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle D_{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle=[\{a,b\},\ \{a,b\},\ \{b,c\},\ \{b,c\},\ \{b,c\},\ \{b,c\},\ \{b,c\}].`$ |  |

$`D_{1}`$ has one extra user (first position) with $`W=\{a,b,c\}`$; the
remaining 7 users are identical and processed in the same order. We
trace the execution of Algorithm 8 exactly.

User 0 ($`W=\{a,b,c\}`$, $`D_{1}`$ only). Histogram is $`(0,0,0)`$.
Gaps: $`G=(5,5,5)`$, $`\left\lVert G\right\rVert_{2}=5\sqrt{3}>1`$.
Solve $`3\lambda^{2}=1`$: $`\lambda=1/\sqrt{3}`$. Each item incremented
by $`1/\sqrt{3}`$.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
H_{1}=(1/\sqrt{3},\,1/\sqrt{3},\,1/\sqrt{3}),\quad H_{2}=(0,0,0),\quad\left\lVert H_{1}-H_{2}\right\rVert_{2}=1.
``` |  |

Users 1–2 ($`W=\{a,b\}`$, both databases). Both gaps exceed
$`1/\sqrt{2}`$. Solve $`2\lambda^{2}=1`$: $`\lambda=1/\sqrt{2}`$. Each
of $`a,b`$ incremented by $`1/\sqrt{2}`$ in both histograms. Difference
unchanged:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
H_{1}-H_{2}=(1/\sqrt{3},\,1/\sqrt{3},\,1/\sqrt{3}),\quad\left\lVert H_{1}-H_{2}\right\rVert_{2}=1.
``` |  |

Users 3–6 ($`W=\{b,c\}`$, both databases). Same analysis:
$`\lambda=1/\sqrt{2}`$, items $`b,c`$ incremented by $`1/\sqrt{2}`$ in
both. After user 6:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle H_{1}`$ | $`\displaystyle=(1/\sqrt{3}+2/\sqrt{2},\ 1/\sqrt{3}+6/\sqrt{2},\ 1/\sqrt{3}+4/\sqrt{2})\approx(1.992,\,4.820,\,3.406),`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle H_{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle=(2/\sqrt{2},\ 6/\sqrt{2},\ 4/\sqrt{2})\approx(1.414,\,4.243,\,2.828).`$ |  |

Difference: $`(1/\sqrt{3},\,1/\sqrt{3},\,1/\sqrt{3})`$,
$`\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}=1`$.

User 7 ($`W=\{b,c\}`$, both databases — the critical step).

*$`H_{1}`$:* Gaps
$`G_{b}^{(1)}=5-(1/\sqrt{3}+6/\sqrt{2})\approx 0.180`$,
$`G_{c}^{(1)}=5-(1/\sqrt{3}+4/\sqrt{2})\approx 1.594`$. Since
$`G_{b}^{(1)}<G_{c}^{(1)}`$, solve $`(G_{b}^{(1)})^{2}+\lambda^{2}=1`$:
$`\lambda=\sqrt{1-(G_{b}^{(1)})^{2}}\approx 0.984`$. Item $`b`$ gets
$`\min(G_{b}^{(1)},\lambda)=G_{b}^{(1)}\approx 0.180`$ (reaching
$`\Gamma`$). Item $`c`$ gets $`\lambda\approx 0.984`$.

*$`H_{2}`$:* Gaps $`G_{b}^{(2)}=5-6/\sqrt{2}\approx 0.757`$,
$`G_{c}^{(2)}=5-4/\sqrt{2}\approx 2.172`$. Both gaps $`>1/\sqrt{2}`$, so
$`\lambda=1/\sqrt{2}`$. Both items get $`1/\sqrt{2}\approx 0.707`$.

Final state:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle H_{1}-H_{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle\approx(0.577,\ 0.050,\ 0.854),`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\left\lVert H_{1}-H_{2}\right\rVert_{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sqrt{0.577^{2}+0.050^{2}+0.854^{2}}\approx\boxed{1.032>1}.`$ |  |

Mechanism of violation. Item $`b`$ reaches $`\Gamma`$ in $`H_{1}`$
(small residual gap 0.180) but not in $`H_{2}`$ (gap 0.757). The
$`\ell_{1}`$-descent allocates $`b`$’s saved budget to $`c`$ in
$`H_{1}`$ (increment 0.984) but not in $`H_{2}`$ (increment 0.707). The
asymmetric allocation increases the $`\ell_{2}`$-distance.

Since this exhibits $`\left\lVert H_{1}-H_{2}\right\rVert_{2}>1`$ for
neighboring databases, no invariant set $`\mathcal{I}`$ satisfying
Definition 1.3 of \[[Gopi et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\] can exist
(Property 2 forces the initial pair into $`\mathcal{I}`$, Property 1
keeps all subsequent pairs in $`\mathcal{I}`$, and membership in
$`\mathcal{I}`$ requires $`\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1`$).
Therefore Algorithm 8 is not $`\ell_{2}`$-contractive. ∎

#### B.3.1 The error in the proof

The proof of Proposition 5.1 in \[[Gopi et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\]
computes the Jacobian of the map $`F(x)=\argmax\sum_{i}y_{i}`$ s.t.
$`y_{i}\leq\Gamma`$, $`\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1`$. At a
generic point $`x`$ with $`\Gamma>x_{1}>\cdots>x_{d}`$, if
$`F(x)_{i}=\Gamma`$ for $`i\leq t`$ and $`F(x)_{i}=x_{i}+\lambda`$ for
$`i>t`$, then

|     |                                                 |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       J_{F}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{0}&\mathbf{0}\\
       B&I_{d-t}\end{bmatrix}
       ```                                              |     |

where
$`B_{ij}=\frac{\partial\lambda}{\partial x_{j}}=\frac{\Gamma-x_{j}}{(d-t)\lambda}`$
for $`j\leq t`$. The proof states this has “block diagonal form” and
concludes $`\left\lVert J_{F}\right\rVert_{S_{\infty}}\leq 1`$.

The matrix is block *lower triangular*, not block diagonal. Its singular
values satisfy:

###### Proposition B.5.

For $`t\geq 1`$ and $`\lambda`$ satisfying
$`\sum_{j=1}^{t}(\Gamma-x_{j})^{2}+(d-t)\lambda^{2}=1`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\left\lVert J_{F}(x)\right\rVert_{S_{\infty}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(d-t)\lambda^{2}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\sum_{j=1}^{t}(\Gamma-x_{j})^{2}}}>1.
``` |  |

###### Proof.

Write $`m=d-t`$. Each row of $`B`$ equals the vector

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
c=\left(\frac{\Gamma-x_{1}}{m\lambda},\ldots,\frac{\Gamma-x_{t}}{m\lambda}\right).
``` |  |

Hence
$`BB^{\top}=\left\lVert c\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\,\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}`$,
which has eigenvalues $`0`$ with multiplicity $`m-1`$ and
$`m\left\lVert c\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\sum_{j\leq t}(\Gamma-x_{j})^{2}/(m\lambda^{2})`$
with multiplicity 1. Since

|     |                                                                |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       J_{F}(x)J_{F}(x)^{\top}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{0}&\mathbf{0}\\
       \mathbf{0}&I_{m}+BB^{\top}\end{bmatrix},
       ```                                                             |     |

its largest eigenvalue is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
1+\frac{\sum_{j\leq t}(\Gamma-x_{j})^{2}}{m\lambda^{2}}=\frac{\sum_{j\leq t}(\Gamma-x_{j})^{2}+m\lambda^{2}}{m\lambda^{2}}=\frac{1}{m\lambda^{2}}.
``` |  |

Therefore
$`\left\lVert J_{F}(x)\right\rVert_{S_{\infty}}=\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(J_{F}J_{F}^{\top})}=1/\sqrt{m\lambda^{2}}`$.
Since $`m\lambda^{2}=1-\sum_{j\leq t}(\Gamma-x_{j})^{2}<1`$ whenever
$`t\geq 1`$, the norm is strictly larger than $`1`$. ∎

###### Remark B.6.

The *eigenvalues* of the lower triangular matrix $`J_{F}`$ are
$`\{0,\ldots,0,1,\ldots,1\}`$, all $`\leq 1`$. The likely error was
concluding that the *spectral norm* (largest singular value) is also
$`\leq 1`$, conflating eigenvalues with singular values.

###### Remark B.7 (Scope).

The $`\ell_{2}`$-descent (Algorithm 7) *is* $`\ell_{2}`$-contractive:
its proof (Lemma 5.2 of \[[Gopi et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\], via
Lemma 5.1) uses a geometric argument that does not involve the Jacobian.
Lemma 4.1 ($`\ell_{1}`$-descent is $`\ell_{1}`$-contractive) is also
correct, as it uses a structural monotonicity argument.

### B.4 A Barrier within the Policy Gaussian Framework

Having established that the $`\ell_{2}`$-descent is the policy among
Gopi et al.’s two proposals with a valid $`\ell_{2}`$-contractivity
proof, we now ask why the Policy Gaussian mechanism is difficult to
improve upon. We do *not* claim an information-theoretic lower bound
over all DPSU algorithms. Instead, we isolate the bottleneck in the
proof of Theorem 5.1 of \[[Gopi et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\]: the
spillover items created by the extra user.

#### B.4.1 Symmetric spillover weights

###### Proposition B.8 (Symmetric spillover budget).

Fix $`t\geq 1`$. Consider $`t`$ previously unseen items whose current
histogram values are equal, and let $`v\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{t}`$ be
the increment assigned to these items by a symmetric update policy with
$`\left\lVert v\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1`$. Then all coordinates of $`v`$
are equal to a common value $`c`$, and

|     |                                |     |
|-----|--------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       0\leq c\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}.
       ```                             |     |

Moreover, $`c=1/\sqrt{t}`$ if and only if the policy spends its entire
$`\ell_{2}`$-budget on these $`t`$ items.

###### Proof.

By symmetry, all $`t`$ coordinates are equal, so $`v=(c,\ldots,c)`$ for
some $`c\geq 0`$. The budget constraint gives
$`tc^{2}=\left\lVert v\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 1`$, hence
$`c\leq 1/\sqrt{t}`$. Equality holds exactly when
$`\left\lVert v\right\rVert_{2}=1`$, i.e., when the full budget is spent
on these items. ∎

#### B.4.2 The support-conditioning bottleneck

###### Theorem B.9 (Spillover bound in the support-conditioning proof).

Consider the proof template of Theorem 5.1 of \[[Gopi
et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\]. Let $`D_{1}\supset D_{2}`$ be neighboring
databases, let $`H_{1},H_{2}`$ be their histograms, let
$`T=\operatorname{supp}(H_{1})\setminus\operatorname{supp}(H_{2})`$ with
$`|T|=t`$, and let the mechanism add independent
$`Z_{u}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})`$ noise and output the released set

|     |                                                           |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       A=\{u\in\operatorname{supp}(H_{1}):H_{1}[u]+Z_{u}>\rho\}.
       ```                                                        |     |

If $`H_{1}[u]\leq b_{t}`$ for every $`u\in T`$, then for the event
$`E=\{A\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(H_{2})\}`$,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Pr[\bar{E}]\leq 1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{\rho-b_{t}}{\sigma}\right)^{t}.
``` |  |

Consequently, this proof template certifies
$`\Pr[\bar{E}]\leq\delta_{\mathrm{spill}}`$ whenever

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho\geq b_{t}+\sigma\Phi^{-1}\!\left((1-\delta_{\mathrm{spill}})^{1/t}\right).
``` |  |

###### Proof.

Let $`p_{u}=\Pr[H_{1}[u]+Z_{u}\leq\rho]`$. Since $`H_{1}[u]\leq b_{t}`$
and the Gaussian CDF is increasing,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{u}=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\rho-H_{1}[u]}{\sigma}\right)\geq\Phi\!\left(\frac{\rho-b_{t}}{\sigma}\right)\qquad\text{for every }u\in T.
``` |  |

Because the noises are independent,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Pr[\bar{E}]=\Pr[\exists u\in T:H_{1}[u]+Z_{u}>\rho]=1-\prod_{u\in T}p_{u}\leq 1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{\rho-b_{t}}{\sigma}\right)^{t}.
``` |  |

Solving the right-hand side inequality

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{\rho-b_{t}}{\sigma}\right)^{t}\leq\delta_{\mathrm{spill}}
``` |  |

for $`\rho`$ gives the stated threshold condition. ∎

###### Corollary B.10 (Why beating Policy Gaussian is hard).

Within the support-conditioning proof of Theorem 5.1 of \[[Gopi
et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\], any symmetric $`\ell_{2}`$-budget-$`1`$
policy that fully spends its budget on $`t`$ equally situated spillover
items yields the threshold requirement

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}+\sigma\Phi^{-1}\!\left((1-\delta_{\mathrm{spill}})^{1/t}\right).
``` |  |

The $`\ell_{2}`$-descent attains this case on the corresponding
equal-spillover/full-budget instances; for example, if the extra user’s
active coordinates are exactly those $`t`$ fresh items and their
distance to the cutoff vector $`(\Gamma,\ldots,\Gamma)`$ is at least
$`1`$, then the update spends its full unit budget and splits it
uniformly across them. Therefore, within this proof template and this
equal-spillover/full-budget regime, there is no way to improve the
spillover term without either:

1.  1.
    giving some fresh items less than $`1/\sqrt{t}`$ weight, which
    lowers their probability $`1-\Phi((\rho-c)/\sigma)`$ of crossing a
    fixed threshold;
2.  2.
    abandoning coordinatewise thresholding of an
    i.i.d.-Gaussian-perturbed histogram; or
3.  3.
    finding a privacy proof that does not condition on the support event
    $`E`$.

###### Proof.

By
Proposition [B.8](#A2.Thmtheorem8 "Proposition B.8 (Symmetric spillover budget). ‣ B.4.1 Symmetric spillover weights ‣ B.4 A Barrier within the Policy Gaussian Framework ‣ Appendix B On the Limits of Contractive Policies for Differentially Private Set Union ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"),
a symmetric budget-$`1`$ policy can assign at most $`1/\sqrt{t}`$ to
each of $`t`$ equally situated spillover items, and this value is
attained exactly when the budget is split uniformly across them.
Theorem [B.9](#A2.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem B.9 (Spillover bound in the support-conditioning proof). ‣ B.4.2 The support-conditioning bottleneck ‣ B.4 A Barrier within the Policy Gaussian Framework ‣ Appendix B On the Limits of Contractive Policies for Differentially Private Set Union ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
then gives the stated threshold. For the $`\ell_{2}`$-descent attainment
example, the gap vector on those fresh coordinates is a constant
multiple of $`\mathbf{1}`$; if its $`\ell_{2}`$ norm is at least $`1`$,
then a unit step in the normalized gap direction adds exactly
$`1/\sqrt{t}`$ to each coordinate. The last sentence follows because
$`1-\Phi((\rho-c)/\sigma)`$ is increasing in $`c`$: decreasing the
spillover weight reduces the chance that a fresh item survives the
thresholding step. ∎

###### Remark B.11.

This is a barrier theorem, not an information-theoretic lower bound over
all differentially private set-union mechanisms. It explains why the
Policy Gaussian threshold is hard to improve inside the current
symmetric support-conditioning proof template for a
histogram-plus-Gaussian-threshold architecture, but it leaves open the
possibility of fundamentally different mechanisms or privacy proofs.

### B.5 Experiments

We numerically illustrate the size of the spillover surcharge from
Corollary [B.10](#A2.Thmtheorem10 "Corollary B.10 (Why beating Policy Gaussian is hard). ‣ B.4.2 The support-conditioning bottleneck ‣ B.4 A Barrier within the Policy Gaussian Framework ‣ Appendix B On the Limits of Contractive Policies for Differentially Private Set Union ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale").
The benchmark below is *not* a lower bound on all DPSU mechanisms; it is
simply the threshold one would obtain from the same support-conditioning
calculation if the spillover coordinates carried zero histogram mass.

#### B.5.1 Setup

We generate a synthetic Zipf dataset: $`20{,}000`$ users, universe of
$`50{,}000`$ items, popularity $`\propto 1/\mathrm{rank}^{1.07}`$, user
set sizes following a truncated Pareto distribution ($`30{,}531`$ unique
items, $`13{,}796`$ singletons). All experiments use
$`\delta=\exp(-10)`$.

#### B.5.2 Spillover surcharge

Define the zero-mass benchmark

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho_{\mathrm{zero}}=\sigma\Phi^{-1}\!\left((1-\delta_{\mathrm{spill}})^{1/\Delta_{0}}\right).
``` |  |

otherwise it is simply the gap between the worst-case Policy Gaussian

### B.6 Discussion: Why Better Policies Are Hard

Our results identify one concrete obstruction to improving DPSU within
the presently validated contractive framework. We discuss three natural
approaches and where this barrier arises.

##### Better contractive policies.

The $`\ell_{2}`$-descent moves in the direction
$`G/\left\lVert G\right\rVert_{2}`$ where
$`G=(\Gamma,\ldots,\Gamma)-H|_{W}`$, allocating budget proportionally to
gaps. The $`\ell_{1}`$-descent fills items greedily (smallest gap
first), outputting more items per user. However,
Theorem [B.4](#A2.Thmtheorem4 "Theorem B.4 (Proposition 5.1 of [] is false). ‣ B.3 Counterexample to Proposition 5.1 ‣ Appendix B On the Limits of Contractive Policies for Differentially Private Set Union ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
shows the $`\ell_{1}`$-descent is not $`\ell_{2}`$-contractive. One
intermediate variant does collapse to the ordinary $`\ell_{2}`$-descent:
iterative $`\ell_{2}`$-descent with a fixed cutoff and micro-steps,
because while no item reaches $`\Gamma`$ the gap vector remains a
positive scalar multiple of its previous value. This collinearity
argument does not generally extend to escalating cutoffs, where changing
$`\Gamma`$ adds an all-ones term to the gap vector and can change the
normalized direction, so those variants require a separate analysis.

##### Using $`\ell_{1}`$-descent with honest sensitivity.

One repair strategy would be to use the $`\ell_{1}`$-descent with its
true $`\ell_{2}`$-sensitivity $`C>1`$ and recalibrate the Gaussian noise
accordingly. This increases the Gaussian-noise component of the Policy
Gaussian threshold. The spillover term need not scale in the same simple
way, so the net threshold effect requires a separate analysis;
nevertheless, any utility gain from greedier weight allocation must be
balanced against this larger noise penalty.

##### Non-histogram mechanisms.

Our barrier does not rule out sketches, candidate-set methods, or
adaptive query strategies. The point is more specific: on the
equal-spillover/full-budget instances considered in
Section [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 A Barrier within the Policy Gaussian Framework ‣ Appendix B On the Limits of Contractive Policies for Differentially Private Set Union ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"),
any approach that still releases a coordinatewise thresholded Gaussian
histogram and proves privacy by conditioning on the revealed support
inherits the same spillover bottleneck in that proof step. Whether one
can obtain comparable improvements outside that regime remains open.

##### Summary.

The spillover term is the price of discovering items from a
data-dependent support inside the current Policy Gaussian proof. In the
equal-spillover/full-budget regime, a symmetric policy with
$`\ell_{2}`$-budget $`1`$ can place at most $`1/\sqrt{t}`$ mass on each
of $`t`$ equally situated fresh items, and the $`\ell_{2}`$-descent
realizes this tradeoff. Any further improvement for that regime within
the same proof template must either reduce fresh-item weight and accept
lower recall, or avoid the same support-conditioning architecture
entirely.

### B.7 Related Work

The DPSU problem was formalized by \[[Gopi et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\],
who introduced the contractive policy framework. Earlier work on
releasing search queries \[[Korolova et al.(2009)](#bibb.bibx7)\] and
SQL keys \[[Wilson et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx8)\] considered related
problems but with different privacy formulations. For the special case
$`\Delta_{0}=1`$, \[[Desfontaines et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx2)\] gave a
nearly optimal algorithm based on noisy partition selection. The
$`\ell_{1}`$-descent policy has been used in differentially private
$`n`$-gram extraction \[[Kim et al.(2021)](#bibb.bibx6)\]; our
counterexample
(Theorem [B.4](#A2.Thmtheorem4 "Theorem B.4 (Proposition 5.1 of [] is false). ‣ B.3 Counterexample to Proposition 5.1 ‣ Appendix B On the Limits of Contractive Policies for Differentially Private Set Union ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"))
implies that the privacy guarantees in that work may need
re-examination. The Gaussian mechanism calibration uses the exact
characterization of \[[Balle and Wang(2018)](#bibb.bibx1)\]. Our barrier
argument reuses the support-conditioning step from Theorem 5.1
of \[[Gopi et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\]; unlike a genuine lower bound,
it is specific to that proof template.

### B.8 Conclusion

We made two contributions to the DPSU problem. First, we found and
verified a counterexample to the claim that the $`\ell_{1}`$-descent
policy is $`\ell_{2}`$-contractive (Proposition 5.1 of \[[Gopi
et al.(2020)](#bibb.bibx5)\]), and identified the exact proof error
(confusion of singular values and eigenvalues of a block triangular
Jacobian). This corrects the record on which DPSU algorithms have valid
privacy proofs.

Second, we identified a structural barrier inside the Policy Gaussian
proof. For $`t`$ equally situated spillover items, symmetry and an
$`\ell_{2}`$-budget of $`1`$ force per-item weight at most
$`1/\sqrt{t}`$, and the $`\ell_{2}`$-descent attains this bound on the
corresponding equal-spillover/full-budget instances. Thus improving that
part of the Policy Gaussian threshold analysis on such instances
requires leaving the current support-conditioning template, changing the
mechanism architecture, or sacrificing weight on fresh items.

This does not prove information-theoretic optimality of the
$`\ell_{2}`$-descent over all DPSU mechanisms. Rather, it explains why
the particular room for improvement isolated by our barrier theorem is
hard to access with the techniques currently available.

## Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private $`n`$-gram Extraction

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### C.1 Introduction

Differentially private $`n`$-gram extraction is a fundamental primitive
for privacy-preserving NLP \[[KGKY21](#bibc.bibx10)\]. Given a database
of $`N`$ users, each contributing text data, the goal is to release a
large collection of frequent $`n`$-grams (contiguous word subsequences)
while guaranteeing $`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-differential privacy at the
user level. Extracted $`n`$-grams power downstream applications such as
sentence completion, smart reply \[[KK16](#bibc.bibx9)\], and assisted
writing \[[CL19](#bibc.bibx3)\] that are trained on potentially
sensitive data \[[Carlini19](#bibc.bibx2)\].

Kim et al. \[[KGKY21](#bibc.bibx10)\] introduced DPNE, which iteratively
extracts $`k`$-grams for $`k=1,2,\ldots,T`$ using the differentially
private set union (DPSU) framework of Gopi et al.
\[[GGKSY20](#bibc.bibx7)\]. At each level, a weighted histogram is
constructed with $`\ell_{2}`$-sensitivity 1, Gaussian noise is added,
and items exceeding a threshold $`\rho_{k}`$ are released. The crucial
structural insight is *hierarchical pruning*: at level $`k`$, only
$`k`$-grams whose constituent $`(k{-}1)`$-grams were already discovered
are considered.

Despite this, the DPNE baseline leaves substantial utility on the table.
At level $`k\geq 2`$, the thresholds $`\rho_{k}`$ are set to control the
expected number of spurious (zero-frequency) items, but they do not
affect privacy—because the output
$`S_{k}=\{w:\tilde{H}_{k}[w]>\rho_{k}\}`$ is a deterministic function of
the Gaussian mechanism’s output $`\tilde{H}_{k}`$. This observation
opens the door to *non-uniform* thresholds at zero privacy cost.

##### Contributions.

1.  1.
    Frequency-Informed Pruning (FIP). We use the noisy histogram values
    from level $`k{-}1`$ (public outputs) to prune the candidate set. A
    $`k`$-gram whose prefix or suffix barely crossed the threshold at
    level $`k{-}1`$ is unlikely to be a frequent $`k`$-gram. FIP is
    post-processing—zero additional privacy cost.
2.  2.
    Heterogeneous Thresholding (HT). We assign per-item thresholds
    $`\tau(w)`$ based on a *margin score* derived entirely from
    level-$`(k{-}1)`$ public outputs. Crucially, $`\tau(w)`$ is computed
    *before* the level-$`k`$ histogram $`H_{k}`$ is examined and depends
    only on already-released information—*not* on whether $`w`$ appears
    in the current-level data. Items with high-confidence constituents
    receive lower thresholds; items with low-confidence constituents
    retain the base threshold. Because $`\tau`$ is a public function
    independent of $`H_{k}`$, the output
    $`S_{k}=\{w:\tilde{H}_{k}[w]>\tau(w)\}`$ remains post-processing of
    the Gaussian mechanism.
3.  3.
    Negative result: adaptive thresholding is not private. A natural
    alternative to HT would be to condition the threshold on the
    *current-level* data: give observed items ($`H_{k}[w]>0`$) a low
    threshold and unobserved items ($`H_{k}[w]=0`$) a high threshold.
    Unlike HT, this “adaptive” variant makes $`\tau(w)`$ depend on
    $`\supp(H_{k})`$, which is private information. We prove this breaks
    privacy: removing a user can flip an item from observed to
    unobserved, simultaneously shifting its threshold from $`\rho/2`$ to
    $`\rho`$—a jump far too large for the noise to absorb. We give a
    concrete counterexample where the privacy loss ratio exceeds 651,
    compared to $`\leq 1.2`$ for a uniform threshold. The key
    distinction is: *HT’s thresholds depend on public level-$`(k{-}1)`$
    outputs; adaptive thresholds depend on private level-$`k`$ support
    information.*
4.  4.
    Implementation equivalence. We give a formal proof that our
    efficient implementation (which uses Binomial sampling for
    unobserved items) produces exactly the same output distribution as
    the canonical dense mechanism. A previous version using bucket
    quantization is shown to break this equivalence; we correct it by
    grouping on exact threshold values.
5.  5.
    Empirical verification. We audit our code using the
    Steinke–Nasr–Jagielski one-training-run framework
    \[[SNJ24](#bibc.bibx12)\], and honestly report the audit’s limited
    statistical power for threshold-based mechanisms.

Together, FIP and HT form AFP-DPNE (Augmented Frequency-Pruned DPNE),
which is $`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-DP and outperforms standard DPNE by
5–84% across four datasets. We also honestly disclose the tradeoff: the
unified mechanism increases the spurious rate from 0.6% to 8.7% on
Reddit, an inherent cost of applying the same threshold function to all
candidates.

### C.2 Preliminaries

###### Definition C.1 (Differential Privacy \[[DMNS06](#bibc.bibx4)\]).

A randomized algorithm $`\mathcal{A}`$ is
$`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-differentially private if for any two
neighboring databases $`D,D^{\prime}`$ (differing in one user’s data)
and all measurable $`\mathcal{S}`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Pr[\mathcal{A}(D)\in\mathcal{S}]\;\leq\;e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[\mathcal{A}(D^{\prime})\in\mathcal{S}]+\delta.
``` |  |

###### Definition C.2 (Gaussian Mechanism \[[DR14](#bibc.bibx5), [BW18](#bibc.bibx1)\]).

For a query $`f:\mathcal{D}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}`$ with
$`\ell_{2}`$-sensitivity
$`\Delta_{2}=\max_{D\sim D^{\prime}}\|f(D)-f(D^{\prime})\|_{2}`$, the
Gaussian mechanism adds noise $`Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{d})`$
and releases $`f(D)+Z`$. By \[[BW18](#bibc.bibx1)\], this is
$`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-DP if
$`\sigma=\sigma^{*}(\varepsilon,\delta,\Delta_{2})`$ satisfies

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Delta_{2}}{2\sigma}-\frac{\varepsilon\sigma}{\Delta_{2}}\right)-e^{\varepsilon}\Phi\!\left(-\frac{\Delta_{2}}{2\sigma}-\frac{\varepsilon\sigma}{\Delta_{2}}\right)\leq\delta.
``` |  | (3) |

###### Proposition C.3 (Post-processing \[[DR14](#bibc.bibx5)\]).

If $`\mathcal{A}`$ is $`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-DP and $`f`$ is any
(possibly randomized) function, then $`f\circ\mathcal{A}`$ is
$`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-DP.

###### Proposition C.4 (GDP Composition \[[DRS22](#bibc.bibx6)\]).

If mechanisms $`\mathcal{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{A}_{T}`$ are run
sequentially on the same dataset, where $`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$ is a
Gaussian mechanism with noise $`\sigma_{k}`$ and
$`\ell_{2}`$-sensitivity $`\Delta_{2}=1`$, then the composed mechanism
is equivalent to a single Gaussian mechanism with noise $`\sigma^{*}`$
where $`1/\sigma^{*2}=\sum_{k=1}^{T}1/\sigma_{k}^{2}`$.

##### The DPNE framework \[[KGKY21](#bibc.bibx10)\].

The algorithm iterates for $`k=1,2,\ldots,T`$:

Level 1 (DPSU). Each user $`i`$ has a set of unigrams $`U_{i}`$. After
truncating each $`U_{i}`$ to at most $`\Delta_{1}`$ items, define the
weighted histogram
$`H_{1}[u]=\sum_{i:u\in U_{i}^{\prime}}1/\sqrt{|U_{i}^{\prime}|}`$,
where $`U_{i}^{\prime}\subseteq U_{i}`$ is the truncated set.

###### Lemma C.5 ($`\ell_{2}`$-Sensitivity of Weighted Histogram).

$`\|H_{1}(D)-H_{1}(D^{\prime})\|_{2}\leq 1`$ for neighboring
$`D,D^{\prime}`$.

###### Proof.

Removing user $`i`$ affects only their contribution. Let
$`t=|U_{i}^{\prime}|`$. Then:
$`\|H_{1}(D)-H_{1}(D^{\prime})\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{u\in U_{i}^{\prime}}(1/\sqrt{t})^{2}=t\cdot(1/t)=1.`$
∎

Add Gaussian noise: $`\tilde{H}_{1}[u]=H_{1}[u]+Z_{u}`$,
$`Z_{u}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{1}^{2})`$. Output
$`S_{1}=\{u:\tilde{H}_{1}[u]>\rho_{1}\}`$.

Level $`k\geq 2`$. Define candidate set
$`V_{k}=\{(p,u):p\in S_{k-1},u\in S_{1},(u,p[2{:}])\in S_{k-1}\}`$ (both
prefix and suffix must be in $`S_{k-1}`$). Build $`H_{k}`$ on $`V_{k}`$
with the same weighted scheme, add noise, and output
$`S_{k}=\{w\in V_{k}:\tilde{H}_{k}[w]>\rho_{k}\}`$.

###### Proposition C.6 (Privacy of DPNE \[[KGKY21](#bibc.bibx10), Prop. 4.1\]).

DPNE is $`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-DP if: (i) $`\sigma^{*}`$
satisfies ([3](#A3.E3 "Equation 3 ‣ Definition C.2 (Gaussian Mechanism []). ‣ C.2 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"))
for $`(\varepsilon,\delta/2)`$-DP with $`\Delta_{2}=1`$;
(ii) $`\sigma_{k}=\sigma^{*}\sqrt{T}`$ for all $`k`$ (uniform budget);
and (iii) $`\rho_{1}`$ is set so that the probability of any unique item
from a removed user appearing in $`S_{1}`$ is $`\leq\delta/2`$.

Crucially, $`\rho_{2},\ldots,\rho_{T}`$ do not affect privacy—only
utility.

The intuition: at levels $`k\geq 2`$, the output
$`S_{k}=\{w:\tilde{H}_{k}[w]>\rho_{k}\}`$ is a deterministic function of
the Gaussian mechanism’s output $`\tilde{H}_{k}`$. By post-processing
(Proposition [C.3](#A3.Thmtheorem3 "Proposition C.3 (Post-processing []). ‣ C.2 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")),
it inherits the Gaussian mechanism’s DP guarantee regardless of how
$`\rho_{k}`$ is chosen, as long as the choice does not depend on
$`\tilde{H}_{k}`$ or $`H_{k}`$ at the *current* level.

### C.3 Algorithm: AFP-DPNE

#### C.3.1 Frequency-Informed Pruning (FIP)

Standard DPNE constructs $`V_{k}`$ using only the *membership*
information $`g\in S_{k-1}`$. We additionally use the *noisy count*
$`\tilde{H}_{k-1}[g]`$, which is a public output.

###### Definition C.7 (Margin).

For $`g\in S_{k-1}`$, the margin is
$`\text{margin}(g)=\tilde{H}_{k-1}[g]-\rho_{k-1}`$. For a $`k`$-gram
$`w`$ with prefix $`\text{pref}(w)=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{k-1})`$ and suffix
$`\text{suf}(w)=(w_{2},\ldots,w_{k})`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{margin}(w)=\min\bigl(\text{margin}(\text{pref}(w)),\;\text{margin}(\text{suf}(w))\bigr).
``` |  |

Items not in $`\tilde{H}_{k-1}`$ are imputed with
$`\tilde{H}_{k-1}[g]=\rho_{k-1}`$ (margin $`=0`$).

###### Definition C.8 (FIP-Pruned Candidate Set).

Given tolerance $`m\geq 0`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
V_{k}^{\prime}=\{w\in V_{k}:\text{margin}(w)>-m\cdot\sigma_{k-1}\}.
``` |  | (4) |

###### Proposition C.9 (Privacy of FIP).

FIP is a deterministic function of
$`(S_{k-1},\tilde{H}_{k-1},\rho_{k-1},\sigma_{k-1})`$, all of which are
public outputs of level $`k{-}1`$ or algorithm constants. By
Proposition [C.3](#A3.Thmtheorem3 "Proposition C.3 (Post-processing []). ‣ C.2 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"),
FIP incurs zero additional privacy cost.

##### Intuition.

If a $`(k{-}1)`$-gram barely crossed the threshold
($`\text{margin}\approx 0`$), it is likely a low-frequency item boosted
by noise. Any $`k`$-gram built from it is unlikely to be genuinely
frequent. FIP removes such candidates, yielding
$`|V_{k}^{\prime}|\leq|V_{k}|`$. Since the spurious-control threshold
$`\rho_{k}`$ increases with $`|V_{k}|`$, smaller $`|V_{k}^{\prime}|`$
enables a lower $`\rho_{k}`$ and hence more genuine discoveries.

#### C.3.2 Heterogeneous Thresholding (HT)

For $`k\geq 2`$, $`\rho_{k}`$ does not affect privacy
(Proposition [C.6](#A3.Thmtheorem6 "Proposition C.6 (Privacy of DPNE [, Prop. 4.1]). ‣ The DPNE framework []. ‣ C.2 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")).
Standard DPNE uses a *uniform* threshold $`\rho_{k}`$ for all
candidates. We generalize this to *per-item* thresholds.

###### Definition C.10 (HT Threshold).

For $`w\in V_{k}^{\prime}`$, define:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tau(w)=\rho_{k}^{\text{base}}-\underbrace{\min\!\Bigl(\gamma\cdot\frac{\max(0,\;\text{margin}(w))}{\bar{c}},\;\;\tfrac{1}{2}\rho_{k}^{\text{base}}\Bigr)}_{d(w)\;\geq\;0}
``` |  | (5) |

where:

- •
  $`\rho_{k}^{\text{base}}=\sigma_{k}\Phi^{-1}\!\bigl(1-\eta\min(|S_{k-1}|/|V_{k}^{\prime}|,\;1)\bigr)`$
  is the standard spurious-control threshold (Kim et al.
  \[[KGKY21](#bibc.bibx10), Prop. 4.1\]),
- •
  $`\gamma\in[0,1]`$ is the discount factor,
- •
  $`\bar{c}=\text{median}\bigl(\{\text{margin}(w):w\in V_{k}^{\prime},\;\text{margin}(w)>0\}\bigr)`$
  is the median positive margin (defaults to $`1.0`$ if no positive
  margins exist),
- •
  $`d(w)`$ is the discount, capped at $`\rho_{k}^{\text{base}}/2`$.

###### Proposition C.11 (HT is Public).

The function $`\tau:V_{k}^{\prime}\to\mathbb{R}`$ depends on:
(i) margins, computed from $`(S_{k-1},\tilde{H}_{k-1},\rho_{k-1})`$
(public level-$`(k{-}1)`$ outputs); (ii) $`|S_{k-1}|`$ and
$`|V_{k}^{\prime}|`$ (determined by level-$`(k{-}1)`$ outputs and
$`S_{1}`$); and (iii) hyperparameters $`(\gamma,\eta)`$. None of these
quantities depend on the level-$`k`$ histogram $`H_{k}`$ or its noisy
version $`\tilde{H}_{k}`$. Therefore $`\tau`$ is a public threshold
function.

Note that items without a positive margin ($`\text{margin}(w)\leq 0`$)
receive $`d(w)=0`$, hence $`\tau(w)=\rho_{k}^{\text{base}}`$—the
standard uniform threshold.

#### C.3.3 Full Algorithm

AFP-DPNE combines FIP and HT:

1.  1.
    At level 1: standard DPSU with spillover threshold $`\rho_{1}`$.
2.  2.
    At level $`k\geq 2`$: FIP prunes $`V_{k}`$ to $`V_{k}^{\prime}`$;
    compute $`\tau(w)`$ for all $`w\in V_{k}^{\prime}`$ (before seeing
    $`H_{k}`$); build $`H_{k}`$ on $`V_{k}^{\prime}`$; add noise; output
    $`S_{k}=\{w:\tilde{H}_{k}[w]>\tau(w)\}`$.

See
Algorithm [1](#algorithm1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ C.11 Full Algorithm Pseudocode ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
in
Appendix [C.11](#A3.SS11 "C.11 Full Algorithm Pseudocode ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
for complete pseudocode.

### C.4 Privacy Analysis

#### C.4.1 Main Theorem

###### Definition C.12 (Canonical AFP-DPNE at level $`k\geq 2`$).

Given candidate set $`V_{k}^{\prime}`$, margins
$`\{\text{margin}(w)\}_{w\in V_{k}^{\prime}}`$ (public), and histogram
$`H_{k}`$ with $`\ell_{2}`$-sensitivity 1:

1.  1.
    Compute $`\tau(w)`$
    via ([5](#A3.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ Definition C.10 (HT Threshold). ‣ C.3.2 Heterogeneous Thresholding (HT) ‣ C.3 Algorithm: AFP-DPNE ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"))
    for all $`w\in V_{k}^{\prime}`$.
2.  2.
    Draw noise $`Z_{w}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{k}^{2})`$ independently
    for each $`w\in V_{k}^{\prime}`$.
3.  3.
    Compute $`\tilde{H}_{k}[w]=H_{k}[w]+Z_{w}`$ for all
    $`w\in V_{k}^{\prime}`$.
4.  4.
    Output $`S_{k}=\{w\in V_{k}^{\prime}:\tilde{H}_{k}[w]>\tau(w)\}`$.

###### Theorem C.13 (Privacy of AFP-DPNE).

AFP-DPNE is $`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-differentially private for all
$`\varepsilon>0`$ and $`\delta\in(0,1)`$.

###### Proof.

We prove privacy by combining three components.

Part 1: Gaussian composition. At each level $`k\in[T]`$, the histogram
$`H_{k}`$ has $`\ell_{2}`$-sensitivity 1
(Lemma [C.5](#A3.Thmtheorem5 "Lemma C.5 (ℓ_2-Sensitivity of Weighted Histogram). ‣ The DPNE framework []. ‣ C.2 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")).
The noisy histogram $`\tilde{H}_{k}=H_{k}+Z_{k}`$ (where
$`Z_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{k}^{2}I)`$) is the output of a Gaussian
mechanism with noise $`\sigma_{k}`$.

For levels $`k\geq 2`$: The threshold function
$`\tau:V_{k}^{\prime}\to\mathbb{R}`$ is determined *before* level-$`k`$
data is processed
(Proposition [C.11](#A3.Thmtheorem11 "Proposition C.11 (HT is Public). ‣ C.3.2 Heterogeneous Thresholding (HT) ‣ C.3 Algorithm: AFP-DPNE ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")).
Therefore $`S_{k}=\{w:\tilde{H}_{k}[w]>\tau(w)\}`$ is a deterministic
function $`f_{\tau}(\tilde{H}_{k})`$ of the Gaussian mechanism output.
By
Proposition [C.3](#A3.Thmtheorem3 "Proposition C.3 (Post-processing []). ‣ C.2 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"),
$`S_{k}`$ inherits the Gaussian mechanism’s privacy guarantee.

FIP prunes $`V_{k}`$ to $`V_{k}^{\prime}`$ using only level-$`(k{-}1)`$
public outputs
(Proposition [C.9](#A3.Thmtheorem9 "Proposition C.9 (Privacy of FIP). ‣ C.3.1 Frequency-Informed Pruning (FIP) ‣ C.3 Algorithm: AFP-DPNE ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")),
so it also incurs zero cost.

Setting $`\sigma_{k}=\sigma^{*}\sqrt{T}`$ for all $`k`$: by
Proposition [C.4](#A3.Thmtheorem4 "Proposition C.4 (GDP Composition []). ‣ C.2 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"),

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{1}{\sigma^{*2}}=\sum_{k=1}^{T}\frac{1}{\sigma_{k}^{2}}=\sum_{k=1}^{T}\frac{1}{\sigma^{*2}T}=\frac{1}{\sigma^{*2}}.
``` |  |

The composed mechanism is equivalent to a single Gaussian mechanism with
noise $`\sigma^{*}`$ and sensitivity 1, which is
$`(\varepsilon,\delta/2)`$-DP by the Balle–Wang
formula ([3](#A3.E3 "Equation 3 ‣ Definition C.2 (Gaussian Mechanism []). ‣ C.2 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")).

Part 2: Spillover at level 1. When user $`i`$ is removed from dataset
$`D`$ to form $`D^{\prime}`$, user $`i`$’s unique items in $`H_{1}`$
could reveal their presence. Suppose user $`i`$ contributes
$`t\leq\Delta_{1}`$ unique items, each with weight $`w=1/\sqrt{t}`$.
Item $`u`$ appears in $`S_{1}`$ iff $`w+Z_{u}>\rho_{1}`$, i.e.,
$`Z_{u}>\rho_{1}-1/\sqrt{t}`$.

We set:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho_{1}=\max_{1\leq t\leq\Delta_{1}}\;\Bigl(\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}+\sigma_{1}\Phi^{-1}\!\bigl((1-\delta/2)^{1/t}\bigr)\Bigr).
``` |  | (6) |

For each $`t`$:
$`\mathbb{P}[u\text{ passes}]=\Phi\bigl((1/\sqrt{t}-\rho_{1})/\sigma_{1}\bigr)\leq 1-(1-\delta/2)^{1/t}`$.
By a union bound over $`t`$ items:
$`\mathbb{P}[\text{any passes}]\leq 1-(1-\delta/2)^{t/t}=\delta/2`$.
Taking the max over $`t`$ ensures this holds for all possible
contribution sizes.

Part 3: Combining. The Gaussian composition gives
$`(\varepsilon,\delta/2)`$-DP. The spillover gives a $`(0,\delta/2)`$
leakage at level 1. By basic composition:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{AFP-DPNE is }(\varepsilon,\;\delta/2+\delta/2)=(\varepsilon,\delta)\text{-DP.}\qed
``` |  |

#### C.4.2 Implementation Equivalence

###### Proposition C.14 (Implementation = Canonical Mechanism).

The AFP-DPNE implementation produces exactly the same output
distribution as
Definition [C.12](#A3.Thmtheorem12 "Definition C.12 (Canonical AFP-DPNE at level 𝑘≥2). ‣ C.4.1 Main Theorem ‣ C.4 Privacy Analysis ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale").

###### Proof.

We verify the two cases separately.

Observed items ($`w\in\supp(H_{k})`$): The code draws
$`Z_{w}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{k}^{2})`$, computes
$`\tilde{H}_{k}[w]=H_{k}[w]+Z_{w}`$, and includes $`w`$ iff
$`\tilde{H}_{k}[w]>\tau(w)`$. This is identical to
Definition [C.12](#A3.Thmtheorem12 "Definition C.12 (Canonical AFP-DPNE at level 𝑘≥2). ‣ C.4.1 Main Theorem ‣ C.4 Privacy Analysis ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"),
steps 2–4.

Unobserved items ($`w\notin\supp(H_{k})`$): In the canonical mechanism,
$`H_{k}[w]=0`$, so
$`\tilde{H}_{k}[w]=Z_{w}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{k}^{2})`$. Item $`w`$
is included iff $`Z_{w}>\tau(w)`$, with probability
$`p(w)=\Phi(-\tau(w)/\sigma_{k})`$, independently across items.

The implementation groups unobserved items by their *exact* $`\tau(w)`$
value. Within each group $`G`$ of size $`n`$, all items share the same
probability $`p`$ (since they have the same $`\tau`$) and the same true
histogram value ($`H_{k}[w]=0`$), making them *exchangeable*.

The implementation draws $`X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)`$ and selects
$`\min(X,n)`$ items uniformly at random. For exchangeable Bernoulli
trials with identical probability, the joint distribution of the
selection is:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{P}[\text{items }w_{1},\ldots,w_{X}\text{ selected}]=\binom{n}{X}^{-1}\binom{n}{X}p^{X}(1-p)^{n-X}=p^{X}(1-p)^{n-X}
``` |  |

which equals the product of independent $`\text{Bernoulli}(p)`$ trials
summed over all $`\binom{n}{X}`$ subsets of size $`X`$. This matches the
canonical mechanism exactly.

Across groups, the RNG draws are independent. Therefore the
implementation’s full output distribution equals the canonical
mechanism’s output distribution. ∎

###### Remark C.15 (Previous bucket approximation bug).

A previous version used 50-bucket quantization for unobserved items,
replacing each $`\tau(w)`$ with a mid-bucket value
$`\tau_{\text{mid}}`$. This introduces $`\sim`$0.1% relative error per
item and *breaks* implementation equivalence, because items in the same
bucket may have different true $`\tau`$ values, making them
non-exchangeable. Our final implementation groups by exact $`\tau(w)`$
values (finitely many, since margins are discrete and the
median-normalization produces a finite set of discount levels).

#### C.4.3 Negative Result: Adaptive Thresholding is Not Private

A tempting improvement is to use *different* thresholds for observed vs.
unobserved items:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tau_{\text{adapt}}(w)=\begin{cases}\rho-d(w)&\text{if }w\in\supp(H_{k})\quad\text{(``observed'')}\\
\rho&\text{if }w\notin\supp(H_{k})\quad\text{(``unobserved'')}\end{cases}
``` |  |

This would give observed items lower thresholds (easier to discover)
while keeping unobserved items at the high base threshold (controlling
spurious rate).

###### Theorem C.16 (Adaptive thresholding amplifies privacy loss).

There exist parameters $`(\sigma,\rho,\Delta_{0},D)`$ and neighboring
databases $`D_{1},D_{2}`$ such that the adaptive mechanism’s per-item
privacy loss ratio satisfies:

|     |                                                           |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \frac{\Pr[w\in S_{k}(D_{1})]}{\Pr[w\in S_{k}(D_{2})]}=651
       ```                                                        |     |

while the Gaussian mechanism with uniform threshold gives ratio
$`\leq 1.2`$.

###### Proof.

Let $`\sigma=2.54`$, $`\rho=10.0`$, $`\Delta_{0}=100`$,
$`D=\rho/2=5.0`$.

Consider user $`i`$ who contributes $`\Delta_{0}=100`$ items at level
$`k`$, including a unique item $`w`$ that no other user has. Let
$`D_{1}`$ be the dataset with user $`i`$, and
$`D_{2}=D_{1}\setminus\{i\}`$.

In $`D_{1}`$: $`H_{k}[w]=1/\sqrt{100}=0.1`$ and $`w\in\supp(H_{k})`$, so
$`\tau(w)=\rho-D=10-5=5`$.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Pr[w\in S_{k}(D_{1})]`$ | $`\displaystyle=\Pr[\tilde{H}_{k}[w]>5]=\Pr[0.1+Z>5]`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\Phi\!\left(\frac{0.1-5.0}{2.54}\right)=\Phi(-1.93)=0.0269.`$ |  |

In $`D_{2}`$: $`H_{k}[w]=0`$ and $`w\notin\supp(H_{k})`$, so
$`\tau(w)=\rho=10`$.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Pr[w\in S_{k}(D_{2})]`$ | $`\displaystyle=\Pr[Z>10]=\Phi(-10/2.54)=\Phi(-3.94)=4.13\times 10^{-5}.`$ |  |

Ratio: $`0.0269/4.13\times 10^{-5}=651`$, with
$`\ln(\text{ratio})=6.48`$.

Under uniform threshold $`\rho=10`$:
$`\Pr[w\in S_{k}(D_{1})]=\Phi((0.1-10)/2.54)=\Phi(-3.90)=4.87\times 10^{-5}`$
and $`\Pr[w\in S_{k}(D_{2})]=\Phi(-3.94)=4.13\times 10^{-5}`$, giving
ratio $`\approx 1.18`$. ∎

##### Structural diagnosis.

The adaptive mechanism creates a *coupling*: removing user $`i`$
simultaneously (a) decreases $`H_{k}[w]`$ by
$`1/\sqrt{\Delta_{0}}\approx 0.1`$ (a small effect, well within the
noise), and (b) moves $`w`$ from “observed” to “unobserved”, jumping the
threshold from $`\rho-D=5`$ to $`\rho=10`$ (a large effect, *not*
absorbed by noise). The threshold jump is the dominant privacy leakage.

##### Why the unified mechanism avoids this.

In our mechanism, $`\tau(w)`$ depends only on *margin scores from level
$`k{-}1`$*, not on $`\supp(H_{k})`$. Removing user $`i`$ changes
$`H_{k}[w]`$ but does *not* change $`\tau(w)`$. This decoupling ensures
the output $`\{w:\tilde{H}_{k}[w]>\tau(w)\}`$ remains a post-processing
of the Gaussian mechanism.

### C.5 Utility Analysis

###### Theorem C.17 (HT improves per-item discovery probability).

At level $`k\geq 2`$, for each item $`w`$ with histogram value
$`h_{w}\geq 0`$ and discount $`d_{w}=d(w)\geq 0`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Pr[w\in S_{k}^{\text{HT}}]=\Phi\!\left(\frac{h_{w}-\rho+d_{w}}{\sigma_{k}}\right)\geq\Phi\!\left(\frac{h_{w}-\rho}{\sigma_{k}}\right)=\Pr[w\in S_{k}^{\text{uniform}}]
``` |  |

with strict inequality iff $`d_{w}>0`$ (iff $`\text{margin}(w)>0`$).

###### Proof.

$`d_{w}\geq 0`$ since $`\gamma\geq 0`$ and $`\max(0,\cdot)\geq 0`$.
$`\Phi`$ is strictly increasing. Therefore
$`(h_{w}-\rho+d_{w})/\sigma_{k}\geq(h_{w}-\rho)/\sigma_{k}`$, with
strict inequality iff $`d_{w}>0`$. ∎

###### Corollary C.18 (Expected output size improvement).

$`\mathbb{E}[|S_{k}^{\text{HT}}|]\geq\mathbb{E}[|S_{k}^{\text{uniform}}|]`$,
with strict inequality whenever any candidate $`w\in V_{k}^{\prime}`$
has positive margin.

###### Remark C.19 (Spurious rate tradeoff).

For unobserved items ($`h_{w}=0`$):
$`\Pr[w\in S_{k}^{\text{HT}}]=\Phi((-\rho+d_{w})/\sigma_{k})\geq\Phi(-\rho/\sigma_{k})`$.
The unified mechanism may produce more spurious items than standard
DPNE. This is *inherent*: since $`\tau(w)`$ cannot depend on whether
$`w`$ is observed (for privacy), lowering thresholds for high-margin
items benefits all candidates—observed and unobserved alike.

###### Theorem C.20 (FIP reduces threshold).

Let $`|V_{k}^{\prime}|=(1-\alpha)|V_{k}|`$ for some $`\alpha\in[0,1)`$.
Then $`\rho_{k}^{\text{FIP}}\leq\rho_{k}^{\text{std}}`$, with strict
inequality when $`|S_{k-1}|<|V_{k}|`$ (non-saturated regime).

###### Proof.

$`\rho_{k}=\sigma_{k}\Phi^{-1}(1-\eta\min(|S_{k-1}|/|V|,1))`$ is
increasing in $`|V|`$ when $`|V|\geq|S_{k-1}|`$. Since
$`|V_{k}^{\prime}|\leq|V_{k}|`$, the claim follows. ∎

### C.6 Experiments

#### C.6.1 Setup

We evaluate on four datasets:

- •
  Zipf (synthetic): 50K users, 500-word vocabulary,
  Zipf($`\alpha{=}1.07`$) with structured bigram transitions.
- •
  Clustered (synthetic): 20K users, 300-word vocabulary, 10 topics with
  shared phrases.
- •
  Heavy-tail (synthetic): 30K users, 400-word vocabulary,
  Zipf($`\alpha{=}1.5`$) with Markov transitions.
- •
  Reddit (real): 100K users from the Webis-TLDR-17 corpus
  \[[VTBS17](#bibc.bibx11)\], the same dataset used by Kim et al.
  \[[KGKY21](#bibc.bibx10)\]. Statistics: 147,487 unique words; mean
  184.7 words/user.

Parameters: $`T=6`$ levels, $`\delta=e^{-10}`$, $`\eta=0.01`$,
$`\Delta_{0}=100`$ (synthetic) or $`300`$ (Reddit), FIP tolerance
$`m=1`$, HT discount $`\gamma=0.3`$, uniform privacy budget
($`\sigma_{k}=\sigma^{*}\sqrt{T}`$ for all $`k`$).

Baseline: Standard DPNE with uniform thresholds and structural pruning
only (our implementation with $`\gamma=0`$).

#### C.6.2 Main Results

|                     |           |           |            |        |
|---------------------|-----------|-----------|------------|--------|
|                     | Synthetic |           |            | Real   |
| Algorithm           | Zipf      | Clustered | Heavy-tail | Reddit |
| $`\varepsilon=4.0`$ |           |           |            |        |
| DPNE baseline       | 12,876    | 8,871     | 13,136     | 37,161 |
| AFP-DPNE            | 18,220    | 10,322    | 16,916     | 68,498 |
| Improvement         | +41.5%    | +16.4%    | +28.8%     | +84.3% |
| $`\varepsilon=1.0`$ |           |           |            |        |
| DPNE baseline       | 3,766     | 1,304     | 4,280      | 10,264 |
| AFP-DPNE            | 4,222     | 1,364     | 4,535      | 12,977 |
| Improvement         | +12.1%    | +4.6%     | +6.0%      | +26.4% |

Table 3: Total $`n`$-grams extracted (levels 1–6). All numbers are from
seed 42.

Table [3](#A3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ C.6.2 Main Results ‣ C.6 Experiments ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
shows AFP-DPNE consistently outperforms the baseline across all datasets
and privacy budgets. The improvement is largest on Reddit (84% at
$`\varepsilon=4`$, 26% at $`\varepsilon=1`$) because real NLP text has a
large vocabulary (147K words) with highly concentrated unigram
confidence scores, creating many near-threshold bigrams that HT can
rescue. Synthetic datasets have smaller vocabularies (300–500 words) and
less extreme margin distributions, yielding smaller but still
significant gains (5–42%).

#### C.6.3 Honest Disclosure: Spurious Rate Tradeoff

As discussed in
Remark [C.19](#A3.Thmtheorem19 "Remark C.19 (Spurious rate tradeoff). ‣ C.5 Utility Analysis ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"),
the unified mechanism inherently increases the spurious rate.

|               | Total  | Genuine | Spurious | Spur. % |
|---------------|--------|---------|----------|---------|
| DPNE baseline | 37,161 | 36,951  | 210      | 0.6%    |
| AFP-DPNE      | 68,498 | 62,548  | 5,950    | 8.7%    |

Table 4: Genuine vs. spurious breakdown (Reddit, $`\varepsilon=4`$).

Of the 31,337 additional items AFP-DPNE discovers over the baseline,
25,597 (82%) are genuine. The remaining 5,740 are spurious items with
high-margin constituents that receive low thresholds. This tradeoff is
inherent to the unified mechanism: since $`\tau(w)`$ cannot depend on
whether $`w`$ is observed
(Section [C.4.3](#A3.SS4.SSS3 "C.4.3 Negative Result: Adaptive Thresholding is Not Private ‣ C.4 Privacy Analysis ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")),
lowering thresholds for high-margin items benefits both observed and
unobserved candidates.

Mitigation. Users can: (a) increase $`\rho_{k}^{\text{base}}`$ (reduces
both genuine and spurious), (b) reduce $`\gamma`$ to limit the discount,
or (c) post-filter using application-specific heuristics (free
post-processing).

#### C.6.4 Ablation Study

| Variant                   | Total  | vs. full AFP |
|---------------------------|--------|--------------|
| AFP-DPNE (FIP + HT)       | 18,220 | —            |
|    w/o FIP ($`m=\infty`$) | 17,914 | $`-1.7\%`$   |
|    w/o HT ($`\gamma=0`$)  | 12,876 | $`-29.3\%`$  |
| DPNE baseline             | 12,876 | $`-29.3\%`$  |

Table 5: Ablation study on Zipf ($`\varepsilon=4`$, $`\Delta_{0}=100`$,
seed 42).

HT is the dominant innovation ($`-29.3\%`$ without it). FIP contributes
a modest additional 1.7%. The near-zero impact of FIP alone (w/o HT =
baseline) indicates that FIP primarily helps through its interaction
with HT: by reducing $`|V_{k}^{\prime}|`$, FIP lowers
$`\rho_{k}^{\text{base}}`$, which amplifies HT’s discount.

#### C.6.5 Mechanistic Analysis: Where HT Helps

At level 2 on Reddit ($`\varepsilon=4`$):

- •
  $`|S_{1}|=6{,}169`$ unigrams, with high confidence (median margin
  $`=8.1\sigma`$).
- •
  $`|V_{2}^{\prime}|\approx|S_{1}|^{2}\approx 36`$M candidate bigrams,
  of which 1.6M have $`H_{k}>0`$.
- •
  Standard DPNE: $`\rho_{2}\approx 11.8`$, discovers 11,708 bigrams at
  level 2.
- •
  AFP-DPNE: threshold drops to $`\tau(w)\approx\rho/2=5.9`$ for
  high-margin candidates (83% of candidates receive the maximum
  discount). Discovers 32,696 bigrams at level 2.
- •
  HT extra at level 2: $`+`$15,781 bigrams, the vast majority genuine.

HT is effective because natural language has *concentrated unigram
confidence*: common words like “the”, “is”, “and” have very high margin
scores, while rare words have low margins. Bigrams composed of two
common unigrams occupy a “rescue zone” between $`\rho/2`$ and $`\rho`$:
their counts are moderate, sufficient to pass the lower threshold but
not the standard one.

### C.7 Empirical Privacy Verification

We use the one-training-run audit of Steinke, Nasr, and Jagielski
\[[SNJ24](#bibc.bibx12)\]. Given $`m`$ canary users, we include each
independently with probability $`1/2`$, run the algorithm once, score
each canary by $`n`$-gram overlap with the output, and test whether
scores distinguish included from excluded canaries.

Under $`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-DP, the number of correct guesses $`W`$
out of $`r`$ total satisfies $`\Pr[W\geq v]\leq\beta+2m\delta\alpha`$
where
$`\beta=\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(r,e^{\varepsilon}/(e^{\varepsilon}+1))\geq v]`$
\[[SNJ24](#bibc.bibx12), Corollary 4.4\].

| $`\varepsilon`$   | Correct/Total | Fraction | $`p`$-value | Verdict  |
|-------------------|---------------|----------|-------------|----------|
| 1.0               | 161/300       | 0.537    | 1.000       | ✓ PASS   |
| 4.0               | 160/300       | 0.533    | 1.000       | ✓ PASS   |
| 8.0               | 160/300       | 0.533    | 1.000       | ✓ PASS   |
| Broken (no noise) | 100/100       | 1.000    | 0.168       | see text |

Table 6: Privacy audit (Zipf 10K users, $`\delta=e^{-10}`$, $`m=200`$
canaries, 3 runs aggregated).

##### Audit power and limitations.

The audit achieves $`\approx`$53% correct, barely above random. This is
expected: each user contributes weight
$`1/\sqrt{\Delta_{0}}\approx 0.1`$ per item, while the threshold is
$`\rho\approx 13`$—a single canary’s contribution is drowned by noise.

The broken-algorithm sanity check (no noise added) achieves 100% correct
with $`p`$-value $`=0.168`$, failing to reject at $`\alpha=0.05`$. This
is because with $`m=200`$, $`r=100`$ guesses, and the DP envelope at
$`\varepsilon=4`$ allows correct fraction up to
$`e^{4}/(e^{4}+1)\approx 0.982`$. Detecting violations requires
substantially larger $`m`$ (e.g., $`2000+`$) or white-box access to
pre-threshold histogram values.

We include this audit for *transparency*, not as a substitute for the
mathematical proof in
Theorem [C.13](#A3.Thmtheorem13 "Theorem C.13 (Privacy of AFP-DPNE). ‣ C.4.1 Main Theorem ‣ C.4 Privacy Analysis ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale").
The audit provides weak positive evidence—no privacy violation
detected—but its limited statistical power for threshold-based
mechanisms is a known challenge \[[SNJ24](#bibc.bibx12)\].

### C.8 Discussion: The $`\ell_{1}`$-Descent Bug

Gopi et al. \[[GGKSY20](#bibc.bibx7)\] proposed the $`\ell_{1}`$-descent
policy as an alternative to the weighted Gaussian policy for DPSU. They
claimed $`\ell_{1}`$-descent is $`\ell_{2}`$-contractive, which is
needed for the Gaussian mechanism’s sensitivity bound. As documented in
\[[ImDPSU](#bibc.bibx8)\], this claim is *false*: expansion ratios up to
1.44 were found empirically. The $`\ell_{2}`$-descent policy *is*
provably contractive, but $`\ell_{1}`$-descent is not.

Our algorithm uses the weighted Gaussian policy exclusively, which
achieves $`\ell_{2}`$-sensitivity 1 by the Cauchy–Schwarz argument
(Lemma [C.5](#A3.Thmtheorem5 "Lemma C.5 (ℓ_2-Sensitivity of Weighted Histogram). ‣ The DPNE framework []. ‣ C.2 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"))
and does not require contractivity.

### C.9 Related Work

DPSU and DPNE. Differentially private set union was introduced by Gopi
et al. \[[GGKSY20](#bibc.bibx7)\]. Kim et al. \[[KGKY21](#bibc.bibx10)\]
extended it to $`n`$-gram extraction. Our work improves upon Kim et al.
by exploiting the structural freedom in threshold choice at levels
$`k\geq 2`$.

Gaussian mechanism. We use the analytic Gaussian mechanism of Balle and
Wang \[[BW18](#bibc.bibx1)\] for tight calibration, and GDP composition
\[[DRS22](#bibc.bibx6)\] for multi-level privacy accounting.

Privacy auditing. Steinke, Nasr, and Jagielski \[[SNJ24](#bibc.bibx12)\]
introduced the one-training-run audit we employ. Our experience
highlights its limitations for threshold-based mechanisms.

Threshold manipulation in DP. To our knowledge, the negative result on
adaptive thresholding
(Theorem [C.16](#A3.Thmtheorem16 "Theorem C.16 (Adaptive thresholding amplifies privacy loss). ‣ C.4.3 Negative Result: Adaptive Thresholding is Not Private ‣ C.4 Privacy Analysis ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"))
is new. It clarifies that while *public* threshold functions are safe,
*data-dependent* threshold functions (even those depending only on
support information) can catastrophically amplify privacy loss.

### C.10 Conclusion

We introduced AFP-DPNE, which improves differentially private $`n`$-gram
extraction by 5–84% through two zero-cost innovations:
Frequency-Informed Pruning and Heterogeneous Thresholding. Both exploit
the structural property that level-$`k`$ thresholds ($`k\geq 2`$) do not
affect privacy. The algorithm is provably $`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-DP
for all $`\varepsilon>0`$ and $`\delta\in(0,1)`$.

We also proved that adaptive thresholding (different thresholds for
observed vs. unobserved items) amplifies privacy loss by $`651\times`$,
delineating the boundary between safe and unsafe threshold manipulation.
The honest cost of the unified mechanism is a higher spurious rate (8.7%
on Reddit vs. 0.6% baseline), inherent to applying the same threshold
function to all candidates.

##### Limitations.

(1) The spurious rate increase may be unacceptable for some
applications. (2) Improvement magnitude is data-dependent: larger on
data with large vocabulary and concentrated unigram confidence. (3) The
privacy audit has limited power for threshold mechanisms and does not
substitute for the mathematical proof. (4) We evaluate on one real
dataset; broader evaluation would strengthen claims.

### C.11 Full Algorithm Pseudocode

Input: Users $`\{(i,w_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}`$; max length $`T`$; contribution
bounds $`\Delta_{1},\ldots,\Delta_{T}`$; privacy parameters
$`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$; FIP tolerance $`m\geq 0`$; HT discount
$`\gamma\in[0,1]`$; spurious fraction $`\eta>0`$

Output: $`S_{1},\ldots,S_{T}`$

// Privacy budget

1 $`\sigma^{*}\leftarrow`$ BW calibration for
$`(\varepsilon,\delta/2)`$-DP with $`\Delta_{2}=1`$ ; //
Eq. ([3](#A3.E3 "Equation 3 ‣ Definition C.2 (Gaussian Mechanism []). ‣ C.2 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"))

2 $`\sigma_{k}\leftarrow\sigma^{*}\sqrt{T}`$ for all $`k\in[T]`$;

// Level 1: DPSU

3
$`\rho_{1}\leftarrow\max_{t\leq\Delta_{1}}\bigl(1/\sqrt{t}+\sigma_{1}\Phi^{-1}((1-\delta/2)^{1/t})\bigr)`$
; //
Eq. ([6](#A3.E6 "Equation 6 ‣ Proof. ‣ C.4.1 Main Theorem ‣ C.4 Privacy Analysis ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"))

4 for *each user $`i`$* do

     5 $`U_{i}^{\prime}\leftarrow`$ truncate $`U_{i}`$ to $`\Delta_{1}`$
items (random subsample if $`|U_{i}|>\Delta_{1}`$);

     6 for *$`u\in U_{i}^{\prime}`$* do

         7 $`H_{1}[u]\leftarrow H_{1}[u]+1/\sqrt{|U_{i}^{\prime}|}`$;

8 for *$`u\in\supp(H_{1})`$* do

     9 $`Z_{u}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{1}^{2})`$;

     10 $`\tilde{H}_{1}[u]\leftarrow H_{1}[u]+Z_{u}`$;

     11 Include $`u`$ in $`S_{1}`$ iff $`\tilde{H}_{1}[u]>\rho_{1}`$;

// Levels $`k=2,\ldots,T`$

12 for *$`k=2`$ to $`T`$* do

    // Step 1: Structural pruning

     13
$`V_{k}\leftarrow\{(p,u):p\in S_{k-1},\;u\in S_{1},\;(p,u)[2{:}]\in S_{k-1}\}`$;

    // Step 2: FIP pruning
(Def. [C.8](#A3.Thmtheorem8 "Definition C.8 (FIP-Pruned Candidate Set). ‣ C.3.1 Frequency-Informed Pruning (FIP) ‣ C.3 Algorithm: AFP-DPNE ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"))

     14 for *$`w\in V_{k}`$* do

         15
$`\text{margin}(w)\leftarrow\min\bigl(\tilde{H}_{k-1}[\text{pref}(w)]-\rho_{k-1},\;\tilde{H}_{k-1}[\text{suf}(w)]-\rho_{k-1}\bigr)`$;

     16
$`V_{k}^{\prime}\leftarrow\{w\in V_{k}:\text{margin}(w)>-m\sigma_{k-1}\}`$;

    // Step 3: HT threshold
(Def. [C.10](#A3.Thmtheorem10 "Definition C.10 (HT Threshold). ‣ C.3.2 Heterogeneous Thresholding (HT) ‣ C.3 Algorithm: AFP-DPNE ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")),
computed BEFORE seeing $`H_{k}`$

     17
$`\rho_{k}^{\text{base}}\leftarrow\sigma_{k}\Phi^{-1}\bigl(1-\eta\min(|S_{k-1}|/|V_{k}^{\prime}|,1)\bigr)`$;

     18
$`\bar{c}\leftarrow\text{median}\bigl(\{\text{margin}(w):w\in V_{k}^{\prime},\;\text{margin}(w)>0\}\bigr)`$;

     19 for *$`w\in V_{k}^{\prime}`$* do

         20
$`d(w)\leftarrow\min\bigl(\gamma\cdot\max(0,\text{margin}(w)/\bar{c}),\;\rho_{k}^{\text{base}}/2\bigr)`$;

         21 $`\tau(w)\leftarrow\rho_{k}^{\text{base}}-d(w)`$;

    // Step 4: Build histogram on $`V_{k}^{\prime}`$

     22 $`H_{k}\leftarrow`$ WeightedHistogram(users, $`V_{k}^{\prime}`$,
$`\Delta_{k}`$);

    // Step 5: Threshold observed items

     23 for *$`w\in\supp(H_{k})`$* do

         24 $`Z_{w}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{k}^{2})`$;

         25 $`\tilde{H}_{k}[w]\leftarrow H_{k}[w]+Z_{w}`$;

         26 Include $`w`$ in $`S_{k}`$ iff $`\tilde{H}_{k}[w]>\tau(w)`$;

    // Step 6: Sample unobserved items (exact per-item Bernoulli)

     27 Group $`V_{k}^{\prime}\setminus\supp(H_{k})`$ by $`\tau`$-value;

     28 for *each group $`G`$ with threshold $`\tau_{G}`$* do

         29 $`p\leftarrow\Phi(-\tau_{G}/\sigma_{k})`$;

         30 $`n\leftarrow\mathrm{Bin}(|G|,p)`$;

         31 Add $`\min(n,|G|)`$ uniformly random items from $`G`$ to
$`S_{k}`$;

32 return $`S_{1},\ldots,S_{T}`$;

Algorithm 1 AFP-DPNE: Augmented Frequency-Pruned DPNE
````
