### C.14 Additional Experimental Details

##### Spurious rate on synthetic data ($`\varepsilon=4`$).

|            | DPNE baseline |      | AFP-DPNE |      |
| ---------- | ------------- | ---- | -------- | ---- |
| Dataset    | Spurious      | %    | Spurious | %    |
| Zipf       | 69            | 0.5% | 187      | 1.0% |
| Clustered  | 24            | 0.3% | 40       | 0.4% |
| Heavy-tail | 40            | 0.3% | 140      | 0.8% |

On synthetic data, the spurious rate increase is modest ($`<`$1%),
because the smaller vocabularies produce fewer unobserved candidates
with high margins.

##### Per-level output sizes (Reddit, $`\varepsilon=4`$).

The gain is concentrated at level 2 (bigrams), which has the largest
candidate set and the most items in the “rescue zone” between $`\rho/2`$
and $`\rho`$.

##### On the $`\ell_{1}`$-descent bug.

Our implementation uses the weighted Gaussian policy exclusively. The
$`\ell_{1}`$-descent bug
(Section [C.8](#A3.SS8 "C.8 Discussion: The ℓ_1-Descent Bug ‣ Appendix C Heterogeneous Thresholding for Differentially Private 𝑛-gram Extraction ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"))
does not affect our algorithm. The bug is documented in
ImprovedDPSU/AUDIT_REPORT.md in the repository.

## Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### D.1 Introduction

Explainable clustering asks that the final partition be representable by
a simple structured model rather than by an arbitrary Voronoi diagram.
In the axis-aligned decision-tree model introduced by Dasgupta, Frost,
Moshkovitz, and Rashtchian \[[3](#bibd.bib3)\], each internal node tests
a single feature against a threshold and each leaf corresponds to one
cluster. Gupta, Pittu, Svensson, and Yuan \[[8](#bibd.bib8)\] showed
that, in the non-private setting, the price of explainability is
remarkably well behaved for this model: for $`k`$-median it is exactly
$`1+H_{k-1}`$, and for $`k`$-means the best known upper bound is
$`O(k\log\log k)`$.

We focus on a deliberately narrow question: what changes under
differential privacy _when the explainability conversion is
data-oblivious_? Here “data-oblivious” means that once a private
algorithm has selected a reference center set $`C`$, the subsequent
explainability routine sees only $`C`$ and fresh randomness. This
assumption is explicit in the threshold-tree conversions of Gupta et
al., and it is precisely the hypothesis under which differential privacy
and explainability separate cleanly.

The key observation is simple but useful:

> _Data-oblivious explainability conversions are free post-processing
> under differential privacy._

Consequently, the privacy analysis lives entirely in the
center-selection step. The non-private explainability factor is
inherited multiplicatively, but no additional privacy loss is paid for
building the threshold tree. This sharply contrasts with the naive
alternative of privatizing one cut at a time, which would spend privacy
budget across a depth-$`k-1`$ adaptive recursion. It also suggests an
algorithm-design principle: spend privacy once, at the center-selection
stage, and keep the explainability conversion outside the privacy
boundary. Below we quantify why several other natural routes are
provably more expensive.

##### Contribution overview.

The contributions are as follows.

1.  1.  A generic transfer principle converts any private distinct-center
        selector into a private structured clustering algorithm whenever the
        structure is produced by a data-oblivious conversion with cost
        inflation factor $`\alpha`$.
2.  2.  Instantiating this principle with the threshold-tree theorems of
        Gupta et al. \[[8](#bibd.bib8)\] immediately gives private
        explainable $`k`$-median and $`k`$-means guarantees with
        multiplicative factors $`1+H_{k-1}`$ and $`O(k\log\log k)`$,
        respectively.
3.  3.  A finite-domain exponential-mechanism instantiation over distinct
        $`k`$-subsets of a public candidate set $`\mathcal{G}`$ yields an
        explicit additive term with the exact combinatorial range size.
4.  4.  A quantitative design-space analysis shows that the center-first
        route dominates natural alternatives: privatizing each threshold cut
        incurs an additive term scaling as $`(k-1)^{2}/\varepsilon`$ under
        basic composition versus $`k\ln|\mathcal{G}|/\varepsilon`$ for our
        approach, and selecting structured outputs directly inflates the
        exponential-mechanism range by a factor depending on $`d`$ and the
        Catalan number.
5.  5.  A concrete black-box corollary packages any compatible efficient
        private $`k`$-median selector into an explainable algorithm by
        multiplying its utility guarantee by the non-private explainability
        factor.
6.  6.  A lower-bound family shows that purely multiplicative guarantees are
        impossible for every $`k`$, not only for $`k=1`$: even when
        $`\mathrm{OPT}_{1,k}(X)=0`$, some additive privacy tax remains
        unavoidable.

##### Scope and limitations.

We do not claim tight $`k`$-dependent lower bounds, a full
characterization of explainability notions that inspect the data after
center selection, or an intrinsically new non-private explainability
theorem. Rather, the point of this paper is that once a data-oblivious
conversion theorem is available, the private analysis becomes modular
and automatically inherits future improvements in private center
selection.

### D.2 Model and Imported Explainability Theorems

A dataset is a multiset
$`X=\{x^{1},\dots,x^{n}\}\subseteq\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}`$.
Two datasets are _neighbors_ if one can be obtained from the other by
replacing one point. For $`q\in\{1,2\}`$ and a center set
$`C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}`$ with $`|C|=k`$, define

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \mathrm{cost}_{q}(X,C):=\sum_{x\in X}\min_{c\in C}\|x-c\|_{q}^{q},
       ```                                                                 |     |

and let $`\mathrm{OPT}_{q,k}(X)`$ denote the minimum of
$`\mathrm{cost}_{q}(X,C)`$ over all $`k`$-element sets
$`C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}`$.

##### Threshold-tree explainability.

A threshold tree is a binary tree whose internal nodes apply tests of
the form $`x_{i}\leq\theta`$. If such a tree separates a distinct center
set $`C`$, then each leaf contains exactly one center and therefore
induces an assignment of every data point to the unique center in the
same leaf. The resulting cost is again measured in the $`\ell_{q}^{q}`$
objective.

###### Definition D.1 (Data-oblivious center-to-structure conversion).

Fix an objective $`q\in\{1,2\}`$ and a family of structured assignment
rules $`\mathcal{M}`$. A randomized conversion $`\mathcal{E}`$ with
factor $`\alpha`$ is _data-oblivious_ if, for every distinct
$`k`$-center set $`C`$, it outputs a random model $`M\in\mathcal{M}`$
whose distribution depends only on $`C`$, and each such $`M`$ induces an
assignment rule from data points to centers in $`C`$ such that for every
dataset $`X\subseteq\mathcal{D}`$,

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{cost}_{q}(X,M;C)\bigr]\leq\alpha\,\mathrm{cost}_{q}(X,C).
``` |  |

The threshold-tree conversions of Gupta et al. fit this definition
exactly. Throughout, we rely on the FOCS 2023 version of *The Price of
Explainability for Clustering* \[[8](#bibd.bib8)\].

###### Theorem D.2 (Imported explainability theorems from \[[8](#bibd.bib8)\]).

The following source-paper guarantees hold for every distinct center set
$`C`$.

1.  1.
    Theorem 1 of \[[8](#bibd.bib8)\] states that the
    independent-recursion random-thresholds conversion for $`k`$-median
    is data-oblivious and satisfies

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{1}(X,M;C)]\leq(1+H_{k-1})\,\mathrm{cost}_{1}(X,C)
    ``` |  |

    for every dataset $`X`$. Here $`H_{k-1}=\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}1/i`$.
2.  2.
    Theorem 3 of \[[8](#bibd.bib8)\] states that there is a
    data-oblivious explainability conversion for $`k`$-means with factor
    $`\alpha^{\mathrm{mean}}_{k}=O(k\log\log k)`$, i.e.,

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{2}(X,M;C)]\leq\alpha^{\mathrm{mean}}_{k}\,\mathrm{cost}_{2}(X,C)
    ``` |  |

    for every dataset $`X`$.

Both imported theorems are stated for the same $`\ell_{q}^{q}`$ cost
convention used in this paper, and both require the reference centers to
be distinct because the threshold tree must separate them.

### D.3 A Transfer Principle for Data-Oblivious Conversions

The lifting argument is short, but the abstraction it isolates extends
slightly beyond explainable threshold trees.

###### Theorem D.3 (Transfer principle).

Fix $`q\in\{1,2\}`$ and let $`\mathcal{E}`$ be any data-oblivious
center-to-structure conversion with factor $`\alpha`$. Let
$`\mathcal{A}`$ be an $`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-differentially private
algorithm that outputs a distinct $`k`$-center set $`C`$. Define the
lifted algorithm $`\mathcal{L}`$ by

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}(X):\text{sample }C\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(X),\ \text{then sample }M\leftarrow\mathcal{E}(C),\ \text{and output }(M,C).
``` |  |

Then:

1.  1.
    $`\mathcal{L}`$ is $`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-differentially private.
2.  2.
    For every dataset $`X`$,

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{q}(X,\mathcal{L}(X))]\leq\alpha\,\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{q}(X,C)].
    ``` |  |

###### Proof.

Privacy follows immediately because $`\mathcal{L}`$ applies only
post-processing to the output of $`\mathcal{A}`$.

For the utility bound, condition on the sampled center set $`C`$. By the
assumption on $`\mathcal{E}`$,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{cost}_{q}(X,\mathcal{L}(X))\mid C\bigr]\leq\alpha\,\mathrm{cost}_{q}(X,C).
``` |  |

Taking expectations over $`C`$ completes the proof. ∎

###### Corollary D.4 (Preserving private clustering guarantees).

Suppose the private center selector $`\mathcal{A}`$ satisfies

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{q}(X,C)]\leq\rho\,\mathrm{OPT}_{q,k}(X)+\Gamma
``` |  |

for every dataset $`X`$, then the lifted algorithm satisfies

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{q}(X,\mathcal{L}(X))]\leq\alpha\rho\,\mathrm{OPT}_{q,k}(X)+\alpha\Gamma.
``` |  |

###### Proof.

The claim follows by substituting the assumed bound into
[Theorem D.3](#A4.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem D.3 (Transfer principle). ‣ D.3 A Transfer Principle for Data-Oblivious Conversions ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale").
∎

###### Corollary D.5 (Explainable $`k`$-median and $`k`$-means).

Applying
[Theorem D.3](#A4.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem D.3 (Transfer principle). ‣ D.3 A Transfer Principle for Data-Oblivious Conversions ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
with the conversions from
[Theorem D.2](#A4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem D.2 (Imported explainability theorems from []). ‣ Threshold-tree explainability. ‣ D.2 Model and Imported Explainability Theorems ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
yields the following consequences.

1.  1.
    For $`k`$-median,

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{1}(X,\mathcal{L}_{1}(X))]\leq(1+H_{k-1})\,\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{1}(X,C)].
    ``` |  |
2.  2.
    For $`k`$-means,

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{2}(X,\mathcal{L}_{2}(X))]\leq\alpha^{\mathrm{mean}}_{k}\,\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{2}(X,C)],
    ``` |  |

    where $`\alpha^{\mathrm{mean}}_{k}=O(k\log\log k)`$.

In particular, if the selector has multiplicative factor $`\rho>1`$,
then the *overall* multiplicative factor in front of $`\mathrm{OPT}`$ is
$`\alpha\rho`$ rather than just $`\alpha`$.

###### Remark D.6 (Scope boundary and sanity-check example).

The transfer principle applies to any structured clustering notion
admitting a data-oblivious conversion; it is not specific to threshold
trees. As a trivial sanity check, the nearest-center Voronoi rule is a
deterministic data-oblivious conversion with $`\alpha=1`$, so the
definition interpolates between ordinary private clustering and
genuinely structured private clustering. The paper does *not* claim that
every explainability formalism admits such a conversion: once the
structure depends on the private data beyond the selected centers, the
post-processing argument breaks.

###### Remark D.7 (Other privacy models).

Since the proof uses only the post-processing axiom, the same lifting
extends to local DP \[[14](#bibd.bib14)\], shuffle privacy, and any
other model in which post-processing is free. What changes across models
is the attainable selector guarantee, not the lifting proof.

### D.4 Design-Space Analysis: Why Privatize Only the Center Selector?

The transfer principle suggests a selector-first design, but several
alternative routes exist. We next quantify why each is less attractive.

##### Privatize each threshold cut.

A direct approach privatizes the $`k-1`$ adaptive split-selection steps
in the threshold-tree recursion. Under basic sequential composition with
total budget $`\varepsilon`$, each step receives at most
$`\varepsilon/(k-1)`$. Even if every split selects from at most
$`d|\mathcal{G}|`$ candidates with the same per-point sensitivity
$`\Lambda_{q}`$, the exponential mechanism incurs per-step expected
additive cost

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{2\Lambda_{q}}{\varepsilon/(k-1)}\bigl(\ln(d|\mathcal{G}|)+1\bigr)=\frac{2\Lambda_{q}(k-1)}{\varepsilon}\bigl(\ln(d|\mathcal{G}|)+1\bigr).
``` |  |

Summing over $`k-1`$ steps, the total expected additive error is at
least

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{2\Lambda_{q}(k-1)^{2}}{\varepsilon}\bigl(\ln(d|\mathcal{G}|)+1\bigr),
``` |  | (7) |

compared with the center-first tax of
$`(2\Lambda_{q}/\varepsilon)(\ln\binom{|\mathcal{G}|}{k}+1)\leq(2\Lambda_{q}/\varepsilon)(k\ln(e|\mathcal{G}|/k)+1)`$.
The split-by-split route therefore pays an extra factor of order $`k`$
in the additive term. Under advanced composition \[[5](#bibd.bib5)\]
with privacy relaxation to $`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-DP, the $`k^{2}`$
scaling improves to roughly $`k^{3/2}\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}`$, which is
still worse than the $`k\ln|\mathcal{G}|`$ scaling achieved by the
center-first design and additionally introduces $`\delta>0`$. Moreover,
the Gupta et al. explainability factor is no longer inherited as a black
box: a fresh argument would be needed to show that the noisy recursive
cuts still preserve the desired inflation factor.

##### Select a structured model directly.

Running the exponential mechanism over the space of labeled threshold
trees is formally valid, but the range size is

|     |                                                           |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       |\mathcal{T}_{k}|\leq C_{k-1}\cdot(d|\mathcal{G}|)^{k-1},
       ```                                                        |     |

where $`C_{k-1}`$ is the $`(k-1)`$th Catalan number (counting
binary-tree topologies). Hence the additive term contains
$`\ln|\mathcal{T}_{k}|\geq(k-1)\ln(d|\mathcal{G}|)+\ln C_{k-1}`$ in
place of $`\ln\binom{|\mathcal{G}|}{k}\leq k\ln(e|\mathcal{G}|/k)`$. For
large $`d`$, the structured-output route pays an extra
$`\Theta((k-1)\ln d)`$ in the exponent, and the privacy analysis is no
longer modular with respect to the selector.

##### Other routes.

Privately generating the candidate set $`\mathcal{G}`$ may be a viable
systems strategy, but it falls outside the clean finite-domain theorem:
once $`\mathcal{G}`$ is data-dependent, the privacy analysis of the
selector, the conversion, and the candidate-generation stage must be
composed jointly. Jointly searching over center–structure pairs
$`(C,M)`$ couples the geometric optimization and the structure choice
into a single large state space for which no imported non-private
approximation theorem currently exists.

##### Summary.

The center-first route is the only one that simultaneously (i) avoids
adaptive composition, (ii) inherits the source paper’s explainability
factor as a black box, and (iii) yields a finite-domain additive tax
depending only on $`\ln\binom{|\mathcal{G}|}{k}`$. It is the cleanest
provable design we currently know.

### D.5 Finite-Domain Instantiation over Distinct Center Sets

We next record a self-contained finite-domain instantiation. Let
$`\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}`$ be a public
candidate set. Define

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{G}^{(k)}:=\{C\subseteq\mathcal{G}:|C|=k\},\qquad\mathrm{OPT}^{\mathcal{G}}_{q,k}(X):=\min_{C\in\mathcal{G}^{(k)}}\mathrm{cost}_{q}(X,C).
``` |  |

Sampling from $`\mathcal{G}^{(k)}`$ rather than $`\mathcal{G}^{k}`$
ensures that the output center set is distinct, exactly matching the
hypothesis of
[Theorem D.2](#A4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem D.2 (Imported explainability theorems from []). ‣ Threshold-tree explainability. ‣ D.2 Model and Imported Explainability Theorems ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale").

Let

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Lambda_{q}:=\max_{x\in\mathcal{D},\ c\in\mathcal{G}}\|x-c\|_{q}^{q}.
``` |  |

The next lemma identifies the sensitivity required by the exponential
mechanism.

###### Lemma D.8 (Replace-one sensitivity).

For the score function $`s(X,C):=-\mathrm{cost}_{q}(X,C)`$ on the range
$`\mathcal{G}^{(k)}`$, the replace-one sensitivity is at most
$`\Lambda_{q}`$: for every neighboring pair $`X,X^{\prime}`$ and every
$`C\in\mathcal{G}^{(k)}`$,

|     |                                          |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       |s(X,C)-s(X^{\prime},C)|\leq\Lambda_{q}.
       ```                                       |     |

###### Proof.

The two datasets differ in exactly one point, say $`x`$ versus
$`x^{\prime}`$. Hence

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
|s(X,C)-s(X^{\prime},C)|=\left|\min_{c\in C}\|x-c\|_{q}^{q}-\min_{c\in C}\|x^{\prime}-c\|_{q}^{q}\right|\leq\max_{z\in\{x,x^{\prime}\}}\min_{c\in C}\|z-c\|_{q}^{q}\leq\Lambda_{q}.
``` |  |

∎

###### Proposition D.9 (Exponential mechanism over distinct $`k`$-subsets).

The exponential mechanism on the range $`\mathcal{G}^{(k)}`$ with score
$`s(X,C)=-\mathrm{cost}_{q}(X,C)`$ and sensitivity bound $`\Lambda_{q}`$
is $`\varepsilon`$-differentially private and outputs a distinct center
set $`C`$ such that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{q}(X,C)]\leq\mathrm{OPT}^{\mathcal{G}}_{q,k}(X)+\frac{2\Lambda_{q}}{\varepsilon}\left(\ln\binom{|\mathcal{G}|}{k}+1\right).
``` |  |

Moreover,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\ln\binom{|\mathcal{G}|}{k}\leq k\ln\!\left(\frac{e|\mathcal{G}|}{k}\right)\leq k\ln|\mathcal{G}|+k.
``` |  |

###### Proof.

Privacy follows from the standard exponential-mechanism theorem together
with
[Lemma D.8](#A4.Thmtheorem8 "Lemma D.8 (Replace-one sensitivity). ‣ D.5 Finite-Domain Instantiation over Distinct Center Sets ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale") \[[11](#bibd.bib11)\].
The range size is $`|\mathcal{G}^{(k)}|=\binom{|\mathcal{G}|}{k}`$, so
the usual tail bound gives, for every $`t\geq 0`$,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{P}\!\left[\mathrm{cost}_{q}(X,C)>\mathrm{OPT}^{\mathcal{G}}_{q,k}(X)+\frac{2\Lambda_{q}}{\varepsilon}\left(\ln\binom{|\mathcal{G}|}{k}+t\right)\right]\leq e^{-t}.
``` |  |

Integrating this tail inequality yields the expectation bound. The bound
on $`\ln\binom{|\mathcal{G}|}{k}`$ is the standard estimate
$`\binom{n}{k}\leq(en/k)^{k}`$. ∎

###### Remark D.10 (Software upper-bound shortcut).

The trivial inequality $`\binom{|\mathcal{G}|}{k}\leq|\mathcal{G}|^{k}`$
gives the simpler bound
$`\ln\binom{|\mathcal{G}|}{k}\leq k\ln|\mathcal{G}|`$, whose gap from
$`k\ln(e|\mathcal{G}|/k)`$ is exactly $`k(\ln k-1)`$. Both are used in
the companion software.

###### Corollary D.11 (Finite-domain private explainable $`k`$-median).

There is an $`\varepsilon`$-differentially private explainable
$`k`$-median algorithm such that for every dataset
$`X\subseteq\mathcal{D}`$,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{1}(X,\mathcal{L}_{1}(X))]\leq(1+H_{k-1})\!\left(\mathrm{OPT}^{\mathcal{G}}_{1,k}(X)+\frac{2\Lambda_{1}}{\varepsilon}\left(\ln\binom{|\mathcal{G}|}{k}+1\right)\right).
``` |  |

###### Proof.

Combine
[Propositions D.9](#A4.Thmtheorem9 "Proposition D.9 (Exponential mechanism over distinct 𝑘-subsets). ‣ D.5 Finite-Domain Instantiation over Distinct Center Sets ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
and [D.5](#A4.Thmtheorem5 "Corollary D.5 (Explainable 𝑘-median and 𝑘-means). ‣ D.3 A Transfer Principle for Data-Oblivious Conversions ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale").
∎

###### Corollary D.12 (Finite-domain private explainable $`k`$-means).

There is an $`\varepsilon`$-differentially private explainable
$`k`$-means algorithm such that for every dataset
$`X\subseteq\mathcal{D}`$,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{2}(X,\mathcal{L}_{2}(X))]\leq\alpha^{\mathrm{mean}}_{k}\!\left(\mathrm{OPT}^{\mathcal{G}}_{2,k}(X)+\frac{2\Lambda_{2}}{\varepsilon}\left(\ln\binom{|\mathcal{G}|}{k}+1\right)\right),
``` |  |

where $`\alpha^{\mathrm{mean}}_{k}=O(k\log\log k)`$.

###### Corollary D.13 (Efficient-selector plug-in).

Let $`\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{GKM}}_{1}`$ denote a polynomial-time
$`\varepsilon`$-differentially private $`k`$-median selector from Ghazi,
Kumar, and Manurangsi \[[6](#bibd.bib6)\] whose published utility
guarantee can be written in the form

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{1}(X,C)]\leq\rho^{\mathrm{GKM}}_{1}(n,d,k,\varepsilon)\,\mathrm{OPT}_{1,k}(X)+\Gamma^{\mathrm{GKM}}_{1}(n,d,k,\varepsilon).
``` |  |

If $`\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{GKM}}_{1}`$ outputs a distinct center set
under the same $`\ell_{1}`$ cost convention, then there is a
polynomial-time $`\varepsilon`$-differentially private explainable
$`k`$-median algorithm such that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{1}(X,\mathcal{L}_{1}(X))]\leq(1+H_{k-1})\!\left(\rho^{\mathrm{GKM}}_{1}(n,d,k,\varepsilon)\,\mathrm{OPT}_{1,k}(X)+\Gamma^{\mathrm{GKM}}_{1}(n,d,k,\varepsilon)\right).
``` |  |

###### Proof.

Apply
[Corollary D.4](#A4.Thmtheorem4 "Corollary D.4 (Preserving private clustering guarantees). ‣ D.3 A Transfer Principle for Data-Oblivious Conversions ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
with the $`k`$-median conversion from
[Theorem D.2](#A4.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem D.2 (Imported explainability theorems from []). ‣ Threshold-tree explainability. ‣ D.2 Model and Imported Explainability Theorems ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale").
The running time remains polynomial because both the selector and the
random-threshold conversion are polynomial-time. ∎

###### Remark D.14 (Compatibility requirements and further plug-ins).

The displayed corollary isolates the only two compatibility checks
needed when importing a selector theorem from the private clustering
literature: the selector’s utility guarantee must be stated for the same
$`\ell_{q}^{q}`$ objective, and the selector must output a distinct
center set to which the imported conversion theorem applies. Under the
same conditions, the identical template extends to other efficient
selectors as well, including the private $`k`$-means results of Kaplan
and Stemmer \[[10](#bibd.bib10)\]. We state the $`k`$-median/Ghazi et
al. corollary explicitly because it already yields a fully polynomial
end-to-end theorem with the exact $`(1+H_{k-1})`$ explainability factor.
For selectors whose outputs are absolutely continuous in the center
coordinates, exact collisions occur with probability zero, so the
distinct-center hypothesis is typically automatic; discretized or
snapped selectors must verify it separately. More generally,
[Definition D.1](#A4.Thmtheorem1 "Definition D.1 (Data-oblivious center-to-structure conversion). ‣ Threshold-tree explainability. ‣ D.2 Model and Imported Explainability Theorems ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
is semantic rather than algorithmic: for practical use, one also wants
the conversion itself to be computable efficiently, as in the
threshold-tree case. In particular, any compatible selector theorem of
the form
$`O(1)\cdot\mathrm{OPT}_{1,k}(X)+\mathrm{poly}(d,k,1/\varepsilon,\log n)`$
immediately yields an explainable bound of the form
$`(1+H_{k-1})\!\left(O(1)\cdot\mathrm{OPT}_{1,k}(X)+\mathrm{poly}(d,k,1/\varepsilon,\log n)\right)`$.

###### Remark D.15 (Concrete plug-in illustration).

To make the plug-in corollary tangible, consider a private $`k`$-median
selector with multiplicative constant $`\rho`$ and additive term
$`\Gamma`$.
[Corollary D.4](#A4.Thmtheorem4 "Corollary D.4 (Preserving private clustering guarantees). ‣ D.3 A Transfer Principle for Data-Oblivious Conversions ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
gives an explainable guarantee of
$`(1+H_{k-1})\!\bigl(\rho\,\mathrm{OPT}+\Gamma\bigr)`$. The
explainability overhead $`(1+H_{k-1})`$ is moderate and grows only
logarithmically with $`k`$:

| $`k`$ | $`1+H_{k-1}`$ | Lifted mult. $`\rho^{\prime}=(1+H_{k-1})\rho`$ | Lifted add. $`\Gamma^{\prime}=(1+H_{k-1})\Gamma`$ |
|----|----|----|----|
| $`2`$ | $`2.000`$ | $`2.0\,\rho`$ | $`2.0\,\Gamma`$ |
| $`3`$ | $`2.500`$ | $`2.5\,\rho`$ | $`2.5\,\Gamma`$ |
| $`5`$ | $`3.083`$ | $`3.1\,\rho`$ | $`3.1\,\Gamma`$ |
| $`10`$ | $`3.829`$ | $`3.8\,\rho`$ | $`3.8\,\Gamma`$ |

This table does not evaluate the theorem-internal constants of Ghazi et
al. \[[6](#bibd.bib6)\], which would require re-deriving their additive
term under the $`\ell_{1}`$ convention and the distinct-center
hypothesis; we leave that concrete instantiation for future work.

###### Remark D.16 (Public-domain assumption).

The quantity $`\Lambda_{q}`$ is a valid privacy certificate only for
datasets lying in the declared public domain $`\mathcal{D}`$.
Accordingly, an implementation that derives $`\Lambda_{q}`$ from a
public description of $`\mathcal{D}`$ must either validate that all
points lie in $`\mathcal{D}`$ or explicitly clip points into
$`\mathcal{D}`$ before using the sensitivity bound. If the software
instead accepts a user-supplied public sensitivity certificate, then the
burden of validating that certificate rests with the caller. Absent one
of these two contracts, the finite-domain theorem does not certify
differential privacy.

### D.6 An Additive Privacy Tax Is Unavoidable

The transfer principle preserves multiplicative explainability factors,
but it does not remove the additive price imposed by privacy itself. The
key point is that the basic two-point ambiguity persists even when the
algorithm is allowed to output more than one center.

###### Theorem D.17 (Additive lower bound for every $`k`$).

Fix an integer $`k\geq 1`$ and a parameter $`\Delta>0`$. Let
$`\mathcal{M}`$ be any $`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-differentially private
algorithm that outputs $`k`$ (not necessarily distinct) centers in
$`\mathbb{R}`$. Define the neighboring datasets

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
X^{(k)}_{0}:=\{0,4\Delta,8\Delta,\ldots,4(k-1)\Delta\},\qquad X^{(k)}_{\Delta}:=\{\Delta,4\Delta,8\Delta,\ldots,4(k-1)\Delta\}.
``` |  |

Then for at least one $`X\in\{X^{(k)}_{0},X^{(k)}_{\Delta}\}`$,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{1}(X,\mathcal{M}(X))]\geq\frac{(1-\delta)\Delta}{1+e^{\varepsilon}}.
``` |  |

Moreover,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{OPT}_{1,k}(X^{(k)}_{0})=\mathrm{OPT}_{1,k}(X^{(k)}_{\Delta})=0.
``` |  |

Consequently, for every $`k\geq 1`$, no private algorithm can satisfy a
purely multiplicative guarantee of the form
$`\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{1}(X,\mathcal{M}(X))]\leq\beta\,\mathrm{OPT}_{1,k}(X)`$
for all datasets $`X`$ and any finite $`\beta`$.

###### Proof.

By clipping each output center to the interval $`[0,4k\Delta]`$ as
post-processing, we may assume the algorithm always outputs $`k`$
centers in that interval. Write the resulting multiset in sorted order
as

|     |                                                               |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       0\leq c_{(1)}\leq c_{(2)}\leq\cdots\leq c_{(k)}\leq 4k\Delta,
       ```                                                            |     |

and abbreviate it by $`C`$. Define the one-center post-processing

|     |                                            |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       T(C):=\min\{c_{(1)},\Delta\}\in[0,\Delta].
       ```                                         |     |

We first claim that for each $`z\in\{0,\Delta\}`$,

|     |                                               |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathrm{cost}_{1}(X^{(k)}_{z},C)\geq|z-T(C)|.
       ```                                            |     |

If $`k=1`$ or $`c_{(2)}\geq 3\Delta`$, then every center except possibly
$`c_{(1)}`$ lies at least $`3\Delta`$ units to the right of the origin.
Since $`z\in\{0,\Delta\}`$, the nearest center to $`z`$ is therefore
$`c_{(1)}`$, so

|     |                                                              |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathrm{cost}_{1}(X^{(k)}_{z},C)\geq|z-c_{(1)}|\geq|z-T(C)|.
       ```                                                           |     |

Otherwise $`c_{(2)}<3\Delta`$. Then at least two centers lie in
$`[0,3\Delta)`$, so at most $`k-2`$ centers lie in
$`[3\Delta,4k\Delta]`$. For each $`j\in\{1,\ldots,k-1\}`$, let

|     |                                     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       I_{j}:=[(4j-1)\Delta,(4j+1)\Delta].
       ```                                  |     |

These intervals are pairwise disjoint, and each contains exactly one
anchor point $`4j\Delta`$ from both datasets. If every $`I_{j}`$
contained some output center, then at least $`k-1`$ centers would lie in
$`[3\Delta,4k\Delta]`$, contradicting the fact that only $`k-2`$ do.
Hence some $`I_{j}`$ is empty, which means the corresponding anchor
$`4j\Delta`$ is at distance at least $`\Delta`$ from every output
center. Therefore

|     |                                                         |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathrm{cost}_{1}(X^{(k)}_{z},C)\geq\Delta\geq|z-T(C)|,
       ```                                                      |     |

because $`T(C)\in[0,\Delta]`$. This proves the claim.

Now consider the post-processed one-center mechanism

|     |                                                |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \widetilde{\mathcal{M}}(X):=T(\mathcal{M}(X)).
       ```                                             |     |

It is still $`(\varepsilon,\delta)`$-differentially private and always
outputs a point in $`[0,\Delta]`$. Let $`\mu_{0}`$ and $`\mu_{\Delta}`$
be the output distributions of $`\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}`$ on
$`X^{(k)}_{0}`$ and $`X^{(k)}_{\Delta}`$, and let $`F_{0},F_{\Delta}`$
be the corresponding CDFs on $`[0,\Delta]`$. Differential privacy
implies that for every $`t\in[0,\Delta]`$,

|     |                                                   |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       F_{0}(t)\leq e^{\varepsilon}F_{\Delta}(t)+\delta.
       ```                                                |     |

Define

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a:=\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\mu_{0}}[c],\qquad b:=\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\mu_{\Delta}}[\Delta-c].
``` |  |

Then $`a=\mathbb{E}[|0-\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}(X^{(k)}_{0})|]`$ and
$`b=\mathbb{E}[|\Delta-\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}(X^{(k)}_{\Delta})|]`$.
Using the layer-cake representation,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a=\int_{0}^{\Delta}(1-F_{0}(t))\,dt\geq\int_{0}^{\Delta}(1-\delta-e^{\varepsilon}F_{\Delta}(t))\,dt=(1-\delta)\Delta-e^{\varepsilon}b.
``` |  |

Hence $`a+e^{\varepsilon}b\geq(1-\delta)\Delta`$, which implies

|     |                                                            |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \max\{a,b\}\geq\frac{(1-\delta)\Delta}{1+e^{\varepsilon}}.
       ```                                                         |     |

The claim above implies

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\max\!\left\{\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{1}(X^{(k)}_{0},\mathcal{M}(X^{(k)}_{0}))],\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{1}(X^{(k)}_{\Delta},\mathcal{M}(X^{(k)}_{\Delta}))]\right\}\geq\frac{(1-\delta)\Delta}{1+e^{\varepsilon}}.
``` |  |

Finally, both datasets have $`k`$ distinct points, so choosing those
points themselves as centers gives zero cost. Thus
$`\mathrm{OPT}_{1,k}(X^{(k)}_{0})=\mathrm{OPT}_{1,k}(X^{(k)}_{\Delta})=0`$,
and the impossibility of a purely multiplicative guarantee follows. ∎

###### Remark D.18 (Tightness for every $`k`$).

The bound in
[Theorem D.17](#A4.Thmtheorem17 "Theorem D.17 (Additive lower bound for every 𝑘). ‣ D.6 An Additive Privacy Tax Is Unavoidable ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
is achievable for every $`k`$. Define the mechanism
$`\mathcal{M}^{*}_{k}`$ that, on input
$`X\in\{X^{(k)}_{0},X^{(k)}_{\Delta}\}`$, outputs the center set
$`\{R_{\varepsilon}(z_{1}),4\Delta,8\Delta,\ldots,4(k-1)\Delta\}`$,
where $`z_{1}`$ is the first data point and $`R_{\varepsilon}`$ is the
standard $`\varepsilon`$-DP randomized-response mechanism on
$`\{0,\Delta\}`$ (outputting the true value with probability
$`e^{\varepsilon}/(1+e^{\varepsilon})`$). The remaining $`k-1`$ centers
are hardcoded at the anchor locations and do not touch the data, so the
full mechanism is $`\varepsilon`$-DP. A direct calculation shows that
the expected cost on the worse input equals
$`(1-\delta)\Delta/(1+e^{\varepsilon})`$ with $`\delta=0`$. Thus the
lower-bound constant is tight, not merely existential.

###### Remark D.19 (What remains open).

Although tight for each fixed $`k`$, the bound in
[Theorem D.17](#A4.Thmtheorem17 "Theorem D.17 (Additive lower bound for every 𝑘). ‣ D.6 An Additive Privacy Tax Is Unavoidable ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
is $`k`$-independent: it equals $`\Theta(\Delta/(1+e^{\varepsilon}))`$
regardless of whether $`k=1`$ or $`k=1000`$. By contrast, the
upper-bound additive tax from
[Proposition D.9](#A4.Thmtheorem9 "Proposition D.9 (Exponential mechanism over distinct 𝑘-subsets). ‣ D.5 Finite-Domain Instantiation over Distinct Center Sets ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
scales as $`k\ln(e|\mathcal{G}|/k)/\varepsilon`$. The gap therefore
grows with $`k`$ and $`|\mathcal{G}|`$. The present argument constructs
$`k`$-point datasets with $`\mathrm{OPT}=0`$ and reduces to a one-center
mechanism; it does not engage with the combinatorial structure that
might make larger $`k`$ harder. Sharper private-clustering lower-bound
techniques, including the smooth lower-bound framework of Peter,
Tsfadia, and Ullman \[[13](#bibd.bib13)\], appear promising for
establishing $`k`$-dependent or $`|\mathcal{G}|`$-dependent lower
bounds, but we do not currently know how to instantiate them for private
explainable clustering.

### D.7 Related Work and Positioning

##### Explainable clustering.

The threshold-tree model of explainable clustering was introduced by
Dasgupta, Frost, Moshkovitz, and Rashtchian \[[3](#bibd.bib3)\]. Gupta,
Pittu, Svensson, and Yuan \[[8](#bibd.bib8)\] resolved the $`k`$-median
price of explainability and gave the currently best known $`k`$-means
upper bound. The present paper imports their data-oblivious conversions
and studies what happens once the center-selection step itself must be
private.

##### Differentially private clustering.

There is a substantial literature on differentially private $`k`$-median
and $`k`$-means. Early high-dimensional Euclidean-space algorithms were
given by Balcan, Dick, Liang, Mou, and Zhang \[[1](#bibd.bib1)\]. Kaplan
and Stemmer \[[10](#bibd.bib10)\] obtained efficient constant-factor
private $`k`$-means. Ghazi, Kumar, and Manurangsi \[[6](#bibd.bib6)\]
gave nearly best-possible approximation ratios for private clustering
with additive poly$`(d,k,1/\varepsilon,\log n)`$ terms.
Stemmer \[[14](#bibd.bib14)\] studied the local-DP analogue. Our
transfer principle is designed to sit on top of this line of work: any
compatible private center selector can be lifted immediately.

##### Structured private clustering and explanations.

Our scope is deliberately narrow. We do not attempt a complete theory
for every structured or explainable private clustering task. Related
directions include the price of privacy for hierarchical clustering with
provable guarantees \[[9](#bibd.bib9)\] and the price of differential
privacy for hierarchical clustering \[[4](#bibd.bib4)\], differentially
private fair clustering \[[2](#bibd.bib2)\], contrastive explainable
clustering with differential privacy \[[12](#bibd.bib12)\], and
differentially private cluster-explanation systems such as
DPClustX \[[7](#bibd.bib7)\]. These works study different output
structures and different explanation models. Our contribution is a
transfer theorem for the specific but important case where the
structured output is generated from the centers alone.

##### Lower bounds.

The additive barrier in
[Theorem D.17](#A4.Thmtheorem17 "Theorem D.17 (Additive lower bound for every 𝑘). ‣ D.6 An Additive Privacy Tax Is Unavoidable ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
now persists for every $`k`$, but it is still only a minimal
obstruction. Stronger lower-bound machinery for differential privacy,
such as the padding-and-permuting fingerprinting-code framework of
Peter, Tsfadia, and Ullman \[[13](#bibd.bib13)\], suggests that much
sharper bounds should be possible for clustering, but deriving such
bounds for the explainable setting remains open.

### D.8 Artifact-Grounded Empirical Sanity Checks

The companion code artifact includes a small experimental suite for the
finite-domain $`k`$-median pipeline. These experiments use only
synthetic one-dimensional data, public candidate sets, and no external
baselines; they should therefore be interpreted as sanity checks rather
than as proof-bearing evidence or broad benchmark claims. Nevertheless,
they address a practical question left open by theorems alone: how
conservative are the analytic bounds on the small instances for which
the exact finite-domain mechanism is computationally feasible?

|  Experiment |  Setting |  Observation |
|----|----|----|
|  Cost ratios |  Six configurations with $`k\in\{2,3,4\}`$, $`|\mathcal{G}|\in\{8,10,12\}`$, $`\varepsilon\in\{0.5,1,2\}`$, and $`300`$–$`500`$ random seeds each |  Mean observed explainability ratios lie between $`1.1341`$ and $`1.2728`$, while the corresponding theoretical factors are $`2.0`$, $`2.5`$, and $`2.8333`$; the largest observed ratio in these runs is $`2.2655`$. |
|  Scaling |  Exact exponential-mechanism runs for $`(k,|\mathcal{G}|)`$ ranging from $`(2,10)`$ to $`(6,18)`$ |  Average wall-clock time rises from $`0.0035`$s for $`\binom{10}{2}=45`$ subsets to $`2.8905`$s for $`\binom{18}{6}=18564`$ subsets, illustrating the expected combinatorial bottleneck of exhaustive finite-domain selection. |
|  Privacy–utility |  Fixed $`(k,|\mathcal{G}|)=(3,10)`$ with $`200`$ seeds per privacy level and $`\varepsilon`$ ranging from $`0.1`$ to $`10`$ |  As $`\varepsilon`$ increases from $`0.1`$ to $`10`$, the mean selection cost drops from $`1025.4`$ to $`600.1`$ and the exact additive tax drops from $`11575.0`$ to $`115.7`$, matching the expected $`1/\varepsilon`$ trend. |

Table 8: Synthetic one-dimensional sanity checks from the companion
artifact’s experimental suite. These numbers come directly from the
committed experiment results file and are included only to illustrate
the small-scale behavior of the finite-domain $`k`$-median pipeline.

These experiments support three modest conclusions. First, on these
small synthetic instances the observed explainability surcharge is
substantially below the worst-case harmonic upper bound. Second, the
exact finite-domain baseline becomes expensive once
$`\binom{|\mathcal{G}|}{k}`$ reaches the tens of thousands, reinforcing
the motivation for the efficient-selector plug-in results. Third, the
privacy–utility tradeoff moves in the expected direction, with both the
analytic tax and the realized selection cost improving as
$`\varepsilon`$ grows. Because the artifact currently implements only
the $`k`$-median path, we do not present analogous empirical claims for
the $`k`$-means corollary.

### D.9 Discussion

The paper establishes a modular framework for private explainable
clustering in the data-oblivious regime: a transfer principle that
separates privacy from explainability, a finite-domain instantiation, a
design-space analysis quantifying why the center-first route dominates
natural alternatives, and a tight all-$`k`$ lower-bound family showing
that some additive privacy tax is unavoidable. The core theorem is
short, but the design-space comparison in
[Equation 7](#A4.E7 "In Privatize each threshold cut. ‣ D.4 Design-Space Analysis: Why Privatize Only the Center Selector? ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale")
demonstrates that the center-first approach saves an order-$`k`$ factor
in the additive term over split-by-split privatization.

##### Scope and limitations.

The main transfer principle
([Theorem D.3](#A4.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem D.3 (Transfer principle). ‣ D.3 A Transfer Principle for Data-Oblivious Conversions ‣ Appendix D Data-Oblivious Explainability Is Free for Scalable Approximate Clustering ‣ Early Discoveries of Algorithmist I:Promise of Provable Algorithm Synthesis at Scale"))
uses only the post-processing axiom, so its proof is structurally
simple. The paper’s technical depth lies instead in the quantitative
design-space analysis, the all-$`k`$ lower bound, and the careful
integration of these components into a complete framework. Threshold
trees remain the only non-trivial conversion for which we demonstrate
the framework; whether other center-induced structures (balanced split
trees, constrained-assignment templates) admit data-oblivious
conversions with provable inflation factors is an open question.

##### Open directions.

1.  1.
    Prove lower bounds with explicit dependence on $`k`$, $`d`$, or
    $`|\mathcal{G}|`$ beyond the tight but $`k`$-independent obstruction
    established here.
2.  2.
    Fully evaluate the theorem-internal constants of the strongest known
    efficient private selectors and benchmark the resulting explainable
    algorithms on real-world instances.
3.  3.
    Determine whether other structured outputs admit data-oblivious
    conversions with bounded inflation factors, thereby widening the
    framework beyond threshold trees.

##### Takeaway.

For data-oblivious explainability conversions, the multiplicative price
of explainability is inherited from the non-private setting.
Differential privacy adds its own center-selection tax, but it does not
force an additional payment when those centers are converted into an
explainable structure. The lower-bound family shows that this additive
tax survives for every $`k`$ and is tight, even on instances where
$`\mathrm{OPT}_{1,k}=0`$.
